articles.title: 25 years ago, two strangers met in the twin towers and escaped on 9/11. What happened next?
articles.summary: Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark were two of only four individuals known to have survived above the impact zone in the south tower
articles.body:
He has told the story hundreds of times, but it never seems to fade. If anything, it only becomes more vivid. "Oh, gosh," exclaims Stanley Praimnath, his voice cracking with an "ooooooh!" as if bearing a weight. "It's like reliving that day."

Nearly 3,000 people died in the terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington DC on September 11 2001. But Praimnath and another office worker, Brian Clark, were two of only four individuals known to have survived from above the impact zone in either tower of the World Trade Center. The two strangers met in the smoke and fire of the 81st floor of the south tower, and walked down 1,620 steps into the rest of their lives.

Their split-second decisions that day made all the difference. Over the next 25 years, both men moved from middle age into old age and retirement. Both enjoyed family weddings and watched children and grandchildren grow. Both saw US presidents come and go as old wars ended and new wars began . They remained friends through it all.

They also told their story – countless times – in churches, schools, TV studios and elsewhere. "It could be 800, 1,200, a number like that," Clark estimates.

Praimnath, in a separate interview, muses: "People refer to me as 'the 9/11 guy'. It doesn't feel repetitive. It is like unloading baggage from my shoulder, like washing my soul with tears. It is comforting to know that people out there still want to hear."

Clark is now 79, living in retirement in northern New Jersey with his wife; he has 11 grandchildren and two great-grandchildren. Praimnath, a decade younger, lives in Valley Stream, Long Island; he is a pastor, grandfather and empty-nester who speaks of his survival not as luck, but as an act of God's grace.

Their recollections of 9/11 are still as clear as the cloudless sky over Manhattan on that September morning. Clark, a Canadian who was executive vice-president at the financial brokerage firm Euro Brokers, arrived at his office on the 84th floor around 7.15am. Down on the 81st floor, the Guyanese-born Praimnath had settled into his desk at Fuji Bank, where he worked as a loan officer.

At 8.46am, the peace was shattered by a deafening double boom as the hijacked American Airlines Flight 11 slammed into the north tower. Clark recalls: "The lights above me flickered and I spun around in my chair and my peripheral vision caught flames against the window. It was surreal. Two or three seconds later, the flames dissipated and the airspace was filled with singed paper."

Having volunteered as a floor fire warden after the 1993 World Trade Center truck bombing , Clark sprang into action. He retrieved an official torch marked "WTC fire safety team" from an overhead cabinet and began shepherding staff toward the building's central corridor.

Co-workers crowded against the north-facing windows, gazing up nine stories at the raging "ring of fire" consuming their twin building. Thinking the emergency was confined next door, Clark phoned his wife at home and his father in Toronto, reassuring them that he was safe.

Three floors below, Praimnath was on the telephone with a colleague in Chicago who had witnessed the north tower explosion on television and begged him to evacuate. He was looking towards the Statue of Liberty when he spotted another plane – so close that he could make out the "U" on the tail of United Airlines Flight 175 .

"On a given day, it was normal for a plane to zoom by a half a mile to a mile away," he recalls. "But this plane is coming towards me. I made eye contact. I dropped the phone and screamed and said, 'Lord, I can't do this. You take over'. I don't know why I said that – but thank God I said that."

Praimnath dived under his desk in the foetal position, weeping and praying as the Boeing 767 bore down on his window. "With the most thunderous sound, the plane came and crashed into the building," he says.

The aircraft struck diagonally at 9.03am, cutting through the 77th to 85th floors. The impact flattened entire walls, severed electrical wiring and sent a shock wave of jet fuel and debris through Fuji Bank's offices.

Praimnath says: "That big orange glow that you see there – I'm stuck in the middle of it. Upon impact, it looks like a demolition crew came with a big giant wrecking ball and ripped the entire office. Every wall is flattened. I remember a large chunk of the plane was broken off and stuck in the office doorway.

"I remember flames all around me, as if somebody took a giant bag of cement, threw it in the air and I can't breathe. The floor above me collapsed and it's hovering over the desk and I'm like, 'Oh, my God, I'm going to die. It's gonna totally collapse, crush me to death, or I'm gonna get sucked out by the air pressure.' You can hear the sound ."

At the memory, he sets his teeth and blows down the phone to recreate the terrifying whoosh.

Three floors higher, Clark was standing on the west side of the 84th floor when the aircraft sliced into the building's eastern trading floor. "Our room exploded," he says. "Everything came out of the ceiling – air conditioning ducts, lighting, the whole works. For five seconds the building swayed to the west and then it swayed back to vertical. For those 10 seconds I was quite terrified, thinking the building was going to roll over. But it didn't."

When the tower steadied, Clark gathered a group of six or seven colleagues and led them toward the central core. The impact had demolished stairwells B and C, but stairwell A, tucked furthest away on the north-west side, somehow remained open.

The group began descending stairwell A. On the 81st floor landing, they were halted by a man and woman coming up the stairs. "She was insistent we not go down," Clark says. "'No, no, no. You can't go down,' she said and, because she stopped us, it allowed me to hear a call for help from within the 81st floor, a muffled cry: 'Help, I'm buried. I can't breathe.'"

Clark squeezed through an opening where the door frame had been ripped from the drywall and stepped into the dark 81st floor, guided by Praimnath's desperate shouts.

Inside the office, Praimnath prayed for rescue. "I can still remember the flames encroaching and I'm screaming, 'Lord, send somebody, I don't want to die.' I'm crawling away from the flames, dodging all the cables that were hanging in the ceiling, short-circuiting because the sprinkler system came on," he recalls.

"I'm like, 'Oh my God, I'm gonna die.' Somebody had a flashlight on the other end of the floor. The person's saying, 'I'll wait for you', but I couldn't hear because I got temporarily deaf when the plane hit the building. As I'm crawling away, the flames are coming closer, licking up the office space.

"I got to the wall. The person's saying, 'Bang on the wall, I know where you are'. I hit the wall and the person says, 'Climb over there.' It had a hollow ceiling, a 10-foot sheetrock wall, a drywall. I remember that so vividly."

Clark's torchlight had picked out a hand protruding from a hole in the 10-foot sheetrock wall. He grasped Praimnath's hands and hauled him over the partition. The desk beneath Clark gave way, and both men crashed to the floor in a heap.

Clark recalls: "We fell and he gave me a big kiss. I said, 'What's going on, what are you doing?' I stuck out my hand and said, 'I'm Brian Clark.' He says, 'I'm Stanley Praimnath; we'll be brothers for life.' I said, 'Well, I don't have any siblings.'"

Clark noticed that Praimnath had a puncture wound on his palm, while his own hand was cut and bleeding from moving debris. Clark recalls his instinctive gesture of solidarity: "I smooshed our hands together and said, 'In fact, we'll be blood brothers for life. Come on, buddy. Let's go home.'"

When they returned to the stairwell, Clark made the critical decision to ignore the warning of the woman on the landing. Pointing his torch down the staircase, he saw no flames. Clark and Praimnath turned downward. Most of the colleagues who had been with Clark, however, chose to head upward, believing safety lay on the roof. They died in the collapse. At Euro Brokers, 61 of Clark's colleagues perished.

When Clark and Praimnath finally emerged on to the street, police and emergency workers yelled at them to run. Minutes later, the south tower collapsed in a cascade of steel and concrete, sending a rolling cloud of debris surging through lower Manhattan. The two men dived inside 42 Broadway to escape the choking dust.

In the chaos, Praimnath reached into his pocket and handed Clark a business card from a small home business he and his wife operated. Separated in the confusion, Clark used the number on that card to reach Praimnath late that evening, confirming that both had made it home.

While Clark suffered remarkably little long-term psychological distress – describing his lack of post-traumatic stress as an unearned "gift" – Praimnath's return to the living was fraught.

Arriving home on Long Island on the evening of 9/11, Praimnath says he suffered profound memory loss. "I wanted to know what this strange woman was doing in our house with two children, not going home. I refused to go to bed because this strange woman was in that room."

His wife, Jennifer, quietly cared for him without judgment. "She would hobble me into the bathroom, fill the tub with warm water and Epsom salts, and tell me to soak," he says. "Then she would put me on the couch. Every day, she would leave an apple, a sandwich, a bottle of water and a notepad. I don't know how long I was in that state. All I know is that one day, I got up, looked at her, recognised her and snapped out of it."

When Praimnath returned to work in October at a temporary office in Jersey City, he still could not navigate on his own. "I had to draw out my commute on a map and color-code it," he recalls. "When I got to work, people would say, 'Stan, can you please sign this?' I didn't have a clue what I was signing. But they were kind, patient managers. Gradually, the pieces came back."

In the quarter-century since that Tuesday morning, the lives of Clark and Praimnath have remained intertwined. They shared family milestones, celebrated at each other's daughters' weddings and phoned one another regularly.

When Clark's eldest daughter married, Praimnath and his wife were seated at the head table. Praimnath says: "Brian introduced me to all his friends and family as his blood brother. You could see people looking around, thinking, 'Something doesn't quite fit the picture!' But Brian didn't care. That's who he is. He is the big brother I never had."

For Praimnath, surviving 9/11 opened a deep spiritual vocation. In 2006, he became a pastor, joining the staff of the church where his father-in-law was senior minister. Over the past two decades, he has travelled to churches, military bases and schools worldwide, delivering his testimony as a sermon on redemption.

"On 9/11, I was crying out to the Lord under that desk, 'Lord, let me live to walk my daughters down the aisle,' and God answered. I walked Stephanie and Caitlin down the aisle. I've lived to see my grandchildren, Hannah and Ezra. They don't call me Papa – they call me 'Papaya'. Stephanie even bought me a shirt that says 'Papaya'."

Yet Praimnath's resilience has been tested repeatedly. In 1993, he narrowly escaped the first truck bombing at the World Trade Center. He was diagnosed with leukaemia and a severe bout of Covid-19 scarred his lungs with bilateral pneumonia. Then, after a trip to Europe with his wife, doctors discovered that his four coronary arteries were severely blocked, requiring emergency quadruple bypass surgery.

"My question has always been: how many times do you try to kill one man?" asks Praimnath, who retired from the Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation two years ago. "I'm living by grace. I still travel. I still do exactly what I used to do before."

He and Clark know they have more years behind them than lie ahead. On the 25th anniversary , Clark will attend a memorial service at his local town square in New Jersey, beginning at 8.45am, before spending the day quietly with his wife. Praimnath will be at a church in Virginia, telling his story once again, with gratitude.

Both men find themselves speaking to a generation for whom 9/11 is not a living memory, but history. Clark, who retired in 2006, says: "I don't have to teach history anymore – the textbooks have that covered. What textbooks don't have is the emotional reality, the optimism that life carries on despite terrible evil. But whenever I speak at schools, 98% of the time, the very first question the kids ask is: 'Are you still in touch with Stanley?'"

Praimnath experiences the exact same phenomenon. Just recently, he addressed 700 students over Zoom at a Christian school in Tampa, Florida. "These children weren't even alive when the towers fell," Praimnath says. "Yet when you describe the roar of the jet engine and the wing slicing through the office, you can hear the audible gasp in the auditorium. It becomes real to them."

The blood brothers look out at the contemporary US with a mixture of sorrow and perplexity. Clark has become an outspoken pacifist, dismayed by the decades of overseas conflict that followed the attacks.

He says: "With 25 years of time to think about it, I realise more and more the utter futility of war. I think of Germany, Italy, and Japan being our greatest allies today. What on earth are we doing to ourselves? Dropping bombs on residential areas in Ukraine, Russia, Gaza – what a senseless waste of energy and human life."

Clark's aversion to vengeance ran so deep that he was repulsed by the street celebrations following the killing of al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden in 2011. "I was disgusted when people were driving around in pickup trucks chanting 'USA!' and cheering for another human being's death. Capture him, interrogate him, lock him away – fine. But taking lives and celebrating it? No. That is not who we should be."

Praimnath recalls the profound but fleeting sense of unity that blossomed after 9/11. "After that infamous day, the entire nation rallied around each other," he reflects. "All the churches were packed. A month later, everything went back to normal.

"But I still believe we are a resilient people. We may have our political differences but at the end of the day we know that, when tragedy strikes, the labels fall away. On the 81st floor, there were no Republicans or Democrats, no Black or white. We were just brothers trying to find the way out."

articles.title: Police probe deliberate fire at Glasgow tenement amid asylum seeker rumours
articles.summary: The building in Stonyhurst Street, Possilpark - which has been derelict for 20 years - had received £3m to be renovated as affordable homes.
articles.body:
Police are investigating a deliberate fire at a housing association tenement in Glasgow that had previously been targeted by anti-immigration protesters.

The building in Stonyhurst Street, Possilpark - which has been derelict for 20 years - had received £3m to be renovated as affordable homes.

Glasgow MSP Paul Sweeney claimed there was evidence the blaze was started deliberately on Sunday following online "disinformation" that the flats would be used for asylum seekers.

Housing association NG Homes, which owns the block, said these were false rumours and the flats would provide "much-needed" homes for people on its waiting list.

Police Scotland said the fire broke out in a fourth floor flat at about 16:50 on Sunday.

Det Insp Neil Martin urged anyone who saw anything suspicious to get in touch .

"Fortunately no-one was injured but this kind of reckless activity is not acceptable and caused serious disruption in the area," he added.

NG Homes said the damage was still being assessed and it was too early to confirm the impact on the renovation timescales.

Prior to the fire two protests had been held, one in July and another in early August, after it was claimed online that the flats, once refurbished, would be used to house migrants.

Since the blaze, images of the building with flames shooting from the roof have been circulated by right wing social media accounts describing the tenement building as "migrant apartments".

In a post on social media, Sweeney said it was "outrageous" that a refurbished building risked being destroyed by fire in a "socially-deprived community".

He said: "We secured nearly £3m in government investment to bring these tenements back and renovate them, so they can be used for the community in a city with a housing emergency.

"It was never going to illegal immigrants, refugees, asylum seekers - it was never intended for that purpose at all.

"So, anyone claiming that was spreading lies, misinformation, to generate clicks on social media, to whip up the community, wind people up and this is the upshot of it."

Sweeney later told BBC Scotland Radio's Lunchtime Live programme: "Obviously the police and the fire service have to conduct official investigations but, from conversations I had on the street, there were witnesses who said they had seen someone scaling the scaffolding and then a fire materialised on the roof soon afterwards."

Sweeney believes the scaffolding had only been up a few days so the building work had not yet started.

He said the protests in July had been "whipped up by local Facebook groups, speculating about the building being used for asylum seeker accommodation."

This had "provoked a significant picket and protest at the site", he added.

He called for clear communication so that "these conspiracy theorists and malicious actors, particularly from the far right who have got a political agenda to whip this stuff up, are countered effectively".

First Minister John Swinney told BBC Scotland News he had "seen the rumours" circulating about the potential use of the flats for migrant accommodation.

He said anyone involved in setting the building on fire would be apprehended.

"It is completely and utterly unacceptable for any accommodation in any part of Scotland housing anybody to be targeted," he added.

Glasgow City Council said that, working with NG Homes, more than 3,500 empty homes had been brought back to "productive use" in recent years.

It said grant funding for refurbishment came through the Affordable Housing Supply Programme.

Ruairi Kelly, the council's convener for housing and development, said the new housing was intended to be used by people in the community.

"There's the potential individuals have taken it upon themselves to then remove that opportunity from families within the Possil area," he told BBC Scotland News.

He said it was "really difficult" to counteract misinformation, like the suggestion the building would be used to house asylum seekers, because "a lot of people are in a position where they want to believe the worst".

When asked how the council could improve how it addresses such rumours, Kelly said the true plans for the building had reached the people who were spreading misinformation, but they "don't want to hear it".

"It doesn't suit their narrative," he added.

"What suits their agenda is to continue to whip up anger, fear and hatred within communities and set people against each other."

Kelly warned that people could have died in the fire.

"Once a fire has been set, the person who set that has no control over what happens next," he said.

"Thankfully the fire service were in place to put the fire out, but we've seen other fires in the city take hold and be absolutely devastating."

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) said six fire engines and specialist resources had been sent to the blaze on Sunday.

The last appliance left the scene shortly before 14:00 on Monday.

NG Homes was in the process of refurbishing and upgrading a number of buildings on the street.

A spokesperson said: "We are aware that disinformation has circulated regarding the future use of the homes and would once again stress that these claims are false.

"The buildings are being refurbished to provide much-needed affordable homes.

"These properties will be allocated in line with our allocations policy and Scottish housing legislation from our existing housing list.

"As a registered social landlord, we do not allocate housing to people who are not legally eligible for it."

articles.title: China eyes huge naval guns to crush small drones as Trump brings back big battleships
articles.summary: International News: Chinese naval researchers are studying whether high-calibre naval guns could offer warships a low-cost way to counter drone swarms, potentially revivi.
articles.body: Chinese naval researchers are studying whether high-calibre naval guns could offer warships a low-cost way to counter drone swarms, potentially reviving the role of a weapon long associated with the battleship era.According to the South China Morning Post, a team led by Wang Lei of the People’s Liberation Army Dalian Naval Academy has proposed using prefabricated-fragmentation shells that explode near a drone swarm, releasing a cloud of high-speed fragments.The concept would not require the shell to strike individual drones directly. Instead, it would create a wider lethal zone around the swarm, increasing the chances of hitting multiple targets with a single round.The research comes as US President Donald Trump’s proposed Trump-class battleship puts heavily armed surface warships back in the spotlight. The US Navy describes the vessel as a 30,000–40,000-tonne large surface combatant equipped with missiles, hypersonic weapons, electromagnetic rail guns, high-powered lasers and conventional naval guns.The latest Congressional Budget Office assessment puts the planned ship at about 35,000 tonnes. It is expected to carry 128 Mk 41 vertical launch cells, one rail gun, two high-powered lasers and two 5-inch (127 mm) guns.China sees a new role for big guns in the drone ageThe Chinese researchers’ proposal is built around a simple problem: modern warships could face attacks involving large numbers of inexpensive drones arriving simultaneously. Using expensive surface-to-air missiles against individual drones could quickly deplete a ship’s limited supply of interceptors, creating an unfavourable cost exchange for the defender.High-calibre guns could offer another layer of defence. Rather than treating every drone as a separate target, a warship could fire fragmentation shells into the path of a swarm, creating a broad zone filled with high-speed fragments. A single round could therefore have the potential to damage or destroy several drones.The approach could be particularly useful against dense drone formations, where multiple targets are concentrated within a relatively small area. In this role, gun-based interception would complement, rather than replace, a warship’s existing missile-based air-defence systems.The Chinese research points to a possible new role for a weapon once regarded as a defining feature of the battleship era. As drone swarms make naval warfare increasingly dependent on the ability to defeat large numbers of cheap targets, high-calibre guns could give warships a more affordable form of area-based defensive firepower.

articles.title: How rules operate differently for foreign, Indian MBBS graduates
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The National Board of Examinations (NBE) has ruled out lowering the pass percentage for foreign medical graduates (FMGs), saying that “qual.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The National Board of Examinations (NBE) has ruled out lowering the pass percentage for foreign medical graduates (FMGs), saying that “qualifying standards cannot be diluted”.However, when it comes to NEET-PG, the centralised entrance exam taken by almost all Indian medical graduates, the qualifying cut-off has been significantly reduced over the past five years.In NEET PG, percentile cut-off is used, whereas to qualify in FMGE,candidates have to score 50%.The initial cut-off for NEET PG in each of these years has been 50th percentile for the general category, which has been equivalent to roughly 35% marks, and 40th percentile for reserved category, equivalent to about 30%.However, for the sake of filling vacant seats, the cut-off percentile has been reduced every year.It was dropped to zero percentile in 2023 for all categories, which meant that everyone who wrote the exam was deemed qualified including those with negative marks.In 2024, it was dropped to 5th percentile for all, but the equivalent percentage score cannot be calculated because the data on marks was not made public that year.If 50% marks was the cut off for NEET PG, only about 25% of those who appeared would have qualified in the last five years.The proposed single licensing-cum-entrance exam for post graduate seats in India, which would be common for FMGs and for Indian medical graduates, called National Exit Test or NExT, has been postponed indefinitely.NEET PG results raise the question: What share of Indian graduates would be able to qualify in such an exam with 50% and not 50th percentile as the qualifying cut off ?NBE points out that the difference between the FMG screening test and NEET PG is that one is for qualifying to get a licence to practise while NEET PG exam is to rank Indian medical graduates, who have already passed final year MBBS exams, for getting post-graduate seats.Final year MBBS exams are held in the medical colleges where the students have been taught and trained with the inherent vulnerability of institutional bias to boost pass percentages.FMGE was introduced in 2002 by the erstwhile Medical Council of India ostensibly to ensure that doctors trained abroad meet the same standards as those trained in India.The 2002 regulation also made it mandatory for FMGs to complete one-year internship from an institution approved by the MCI after clearing FMGE to get a licence to practise.From Nov 2021, the National Medical Commission, which succeeded the MCI, has mandated that all FMGs, after passing the final year MBBS exam in whichever country have they trained in, have to obtain a licence to practise in that country before they appear for FMGE.While the criteria for an FMG to get a licence to practice in India has been progressively tightened, the opposite has been happening to medical education in India.The infrastructure and faculty norms, and the regulatory oversight for starting new medical colleges in India has been progressively relaxed or diluted to help rapid expansion of MBBS seats.Between 2014 and 2026, the number of medical colleges has jumped from 387 to 818 and the number of MBBS seats from over 51,300 to about 1.3 lakh with complaints piling up of colleges being run without adequate faculty, infrastructure or patient load.Though every candidate appearing for NEET PG is supposed to have passed MBBS with minimum 40% in each subject and 50% overall, candidates scoring single digit, zero or even negative marks in NEET PG puts a question mark over the quality of graduates being churned out from medical colleges in India.It also raises the question, can India have different criteria/double standards for screening FMGs and its own medical graduates given the highly uneven standards of medical education here.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Delhi cops had audacity to go to Bulandshahr, arrest me': 'Influencer' Swatantra to HC; plea rejected
articles.summary: India News: Counsel for self-styled right-wing influencer Swatantra Bhardwaj told the Delhi high court on Monday that the Delhi Police had the \"audacity\" to trave.
articles.body: Counsel for self-styled right-wing influencer Swatantra Bhardwaj told the Delhi high court on Monday that the Delhi Police had the "audacity" to travel to Uttar Pradesh's Bulandshahr and arrest him in connection with the Jantar Mantar protest case."The SC has already quashed all the FIRs and the Delhi Police had the audacity to go to Bulandshahr and arrest me," the counsel was quoted as saying by Bar and Bench.Police, however, contested the claim and told the court that the FIR in the present case had not been quashed by the Supreme Court. The bench then sought a clear response from the Delhi Police, asking it to inform the court whether the FIR was "alive or not" and giving it the option of filing an affidavit or making a statement immediately, Bar and Bench report said.The police counsel also pointed out that Bhardwaj had been produced before a court following his arrest and was subsequently remanded to police and judicial custody.The HC rejected Bhardwaj's habeas corpus plea challenging his arrest in Jantar Mantar assault case.Meanwhile, a Delhi court extended his judicial custody by 14 days till September 21 in connection with the alleged assault on Sanjay Azad during the June 23. Bhardwaj was produced before Special Judge Saurabh Pratap Singh Laler through video conferencing from Tihar Jail after his one-day police custody ended.He was detained in Bulandshahr on September 4 and brought to Delhi, following which a court had on September 5 granted the police one day’s custodial interrogation. He was subsequently sent to one-day judicial custody on Sunday.The arrest followed outrage over a video podcast in which Bhardwaj allegedly claimed that he had "cracked the skull" of Azad during the Jantar Mantar protest and said the alleged assault attracted Section 307. He later claimed he had acted in self-defence. Delhi Police had earlier said Azad's injuries were simple in nature and were caused by a steel bracelet.Police subsequently added provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act and criminal intimidation to the FIR. A separate FIR under the POCSO Act was also registered following a complaint by the teenage activist alleging online threats and harassment after she spoke about the alleged assault on her father.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Malaysia Airlines flight, with 186 passengers onboard, diverts to Chennai after engine snag
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: A Malaysia Airlines flight from Kuala Lumpur to Jeddah was diverted to Chennai on Monday after a technical issue involving one of its engin.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Malaysia Airlines flight from Kuala Lumpur to Jeddah was diverted to Chennai on Monday after a technical issue involving one of its engines, with a full emergency declared at the airport before the aircraft landed safely.Malaysia Airlines flight MH 156 was carrying 186 people when it was diverted. The aircraft landed safely and the airport activated the necessary emergency response arrangements.The technical problem involved "Engine No.2", an airport official said."Further assessment of the aircraft and the technical issue is being carried out by the airline and relevant technical teams," the spokesperson said, adding operations are normal.The aircraft was later moved to a parking bay using a tow vehicle, while the passengers were provided accommodation at the airport.Emergency teams put on standbyFollowing the diversion, the relevant airport operational and emergency agencies were alerted and arrangements were made to handle the aircraft's arrival safely.The aircraft landed without any untoward incident. The airline's technical teams are now assessing the reported engine issue.Airport operations continued normally after the aircraft was brought to the parking area.Air India Express flight also divertedSeparately, an Air India Express flight from Tiruchirappalli to Singapore was also diverted to Chennai on Monday following a technical issue.A "local standby was declared" at Chennai airport and emergency response arrangements were kept ready.The aircraft landed safely and vacated the runway on its own power. The airline's engineering and technical team is assessing the issue."All operations are normal," the official added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Will address colleagues’ genuine concern: Isro chief
articles.summary: India News: BENGALURU: Isro chairman V Narayanan Monday said genuine concerns of his colleagues would be clarified. “...If one or two people give you a letter, on.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Isro chairman V Narayanan Monday said genuine concerns of his colleagues would be clarified. “...If one or two people give you a letter, one cannot give a written communication immediately. Please understand, we are 20,000 employees. But we will address the employees,” he said on the sidelines of Bengaluru Space Expo 2026 here.Narayanan said that Isro had a system to regularly talk to employees. “...For example, when the space sector reforms were rolled out, from the Chairman onwards, we have regularly engaged with our employees,” he added.Earlier at the inaugural, Isro chairman and IN-SPACe chairman Pawan Goenka made a strong case for greater participation by industry, startups and academia in India’s space programme, arguing that the country’s expanding ambitions cannot be met by the national space agency alone.Their remarks came a day after Isro and Goenka had released separate statements about the role of Isro, IN-SPACe and the private sector, which followed a letter by nine employees’ associations raising concerns over the future role of Isro.Narayanan said Monday that India’s requirements were set to rise sharply: “Our space programme is 64-65 years old. Right now, we have 56 space assets in serving the common man of the country. But the [future] need is huge. I think you all know that,” he said, adding that industry would need to play a greater role in meeting that.He said industry had, in any case, long been an integral part of India's space programme. “Whenever an LVM3 is lifting off or a GSLV is lifting off, please do not think that everything is done in Isro. Almost 80% of the budget is invested in Indian industry. About 450 industries are working for us now,” he said.Narayanan said the growth of private companies and startups had to be welcomed if India was to meet its future requirements. From only one or two space startups around the time of the 2020 reforms, the country now has more than 450, he said.But he stressed that greater private-sector participation did not mean a reduced role for Isro. The agency's role was evolving as it took on an expanding range of programmes, including Chandrayaan-4 and Chandrayaan-5, the Venus Orbiter Mission, the Indian Space Station, a next-generation launch vehicle and the expansion of the Navic constellation.India's current capability to launch around 8,500-9,000 kg would also have to be raised to about 30,000 kg, he said. “Isro's role is in no way reduced. But we also have to handhold startup companies and the private sector.”Goenka, meanwhile, said India was building a “full-spectrum space economy” in which Isro, IN-SPACe, Nsil, private industry, MSMEs, academia and investors would play reinforcing roles.From a single space startup in 2014, India now has more than 450, with over $160 million of private investment coming into the sector this year, he said. He urged established suppliers and MSMEs to move beyond supplying components and enter higher-value segments.“You are the quiet backbone of this story today,” Goenka told industry representatives, noting that a substantial share of what Isro builds already comes from its industrial suppliers. He urged them to move “from components to subsystems to full solutions” and serve global supply chains as well.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ASI collects samples from well discovered after mosque demolition in Saharanpur
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: An Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) team on Monday examined a nearly 20-foot-deep well discovered during debris removal at the site of .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) team on Monday examined a nearly 20-foot-deep well discovered during debris removal at the site of a mosque demolished inside the Saharanpur Collectorate premises, officials said.The inspection was aimed at determining the age, nature and historical relevance of the structure, which was found beneath the rubble on Sunday.Heavy police security was deployed around the site and the well was barricaded to prevent access.ASI examines well’s structure and constructionManoj Kumar Yadav of the Uttar Pradesh State Archaeology Department said the inspection was intended to establish the antiquity of the structure and understand its possible historical context."Our primary objective in visiting here was to determine the antiquity of the structure found there. Secondly, we wanted to understand the nature of the structure itself. We also aimed to correlate it with history to understand what it relates to," Yadav told news agency ANI.According to Yadav, the structure appeared to be a well filled with debris that had fallen inside. It was around 20 feet in height from the surface level and had a diameter of nearly three feet."The structure is made using Lakhori bricks. The binding mortar used is a lime-surkhi mixture, and at a depth of three feet from the top surface, there is a thin layer of lime plaster," he said.Yadav added that structures made using similar techniques are commonly found in the Upper and Middle Ganga Valley regions and are generally associated with the later mediaeval period.Three ASI officials reached the site on Monday afternoon and examined the well in the presence of local administration officials. The officials measured its depth after placing a ladder inside and carried out photography and videography.Soil and brick-remnant samples were also collected from inside the well, sadar sub-divisional magistrate Subodh Kumar said.The discovery was made during debris-removal work on Sunday, when workers came across a concrete slab beneath the rubble.The slab was unusually strong. A Pokland machine failed to make a significant impact, after which workers used a cutter and found the brick-lined well.The well was approximately 20 feet deep and around 1.5 metres wide. Its exact age, purpose and historical background were not immediately established.Mosque demolition followed court proceedingsThe well was discovered a day after the demolition of a mosque located inside the Saharanpur Collectorate premises.The district administration demolished the structure in the early hours of September 5 after the mosque committee's appeal against the demolition order was rejected by the district judge's court.The City Magistrate's court had on July 17 declared the structure an illegal encroachment on government land and ordered its demolition. It also imposed compensation of approximately Rs 6.41 crore in connection with the alleged encroachment and misuse of government land.The mosque management committee had challenged the City Magistrate's order in the district court, which rejected its appeal on September 2. Authorities subsequently proceeded with the demolition amid heavy police deployment.Authorities have maintained that the demolition was carried out in accordance with court directions and legal procedures.Claims emerge over well's historical significanceThe discovery has led to differing claims about the possible history of the site.Vikas Tyagi, the complainant in the matter and a former Bajrang Dal convenor, claimed that a temple might have existed at the site before the mosque was built.Saharanpur Congress MP Imran Masood, however, said the well was part of the mosque and had been used in earlier times to meet the requirement for water for wuzu, or ablution before prayers.The ASI examination is expected to help establish the well's antiquity and historical background. Officials have not announced any conclusion about its origin or earlier use.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1956, California burned and demolished the town of Monticello before flooding the valley; 70 years later its streets and homes remain beneath Lake Berryessa
articles.summary: US News: A small California community of ranches, farms, schools and family homes has been covered by water for nearly 70 years. Beneath the waters of Lake Ber.
articles.body: A small California community of ranches, farms, schools and family homes has been covered by water for nearly 70 years. Beneath the waters of Lake Berryessa rests the ghost town of Monticello, preserved in fragments: its roads, foundations and historic bridge still visible beneath the surface while photographs and memories keep its story alive above. The town was flooded as part of a massive water project in California but its legacy has been much harder to wash away. According to The Sacramento Bee, in the 19th century Monticello grew up on Putah Creek in Napa County, and eventually was home to some 300 people. They farmed, raised cattle and created a close-knit rural community in the Berryessa Valley. That life changed in the late 1940s, when the plans moved forward for the Monticello Dam and the reservoir that would be Lake Berryessa. The government bought the land for the project and evicted the residents of Monticello. By 1956, buildings were being destroyed or burned so they would not become hazards when the valley flooded. The dam was finished in February 1957 at a reported cost of $47 million. Soon the valley began to disappear beneath the swelling reservoir, which would provide a major water source for Solano County.What was lost at Lake BerryessaMonticello had more than houses. It had businesses, schools, farmland, community facilities and a popular rodeo with the Scribner family. The valley was also known for its fertile soils that supported cattle, wheat and other agricultural activities. Later, Highway 28, later Highway 128, crossed the southern end of the valley. In 1896 a stone bridge was constructed across Putah Creek joining parts of the community. Much of the land is still under water. During droughts and low lake levels, pieces of the old town have occasionally surfaced, offering a rare glimpse of what was there before the reservoir. The historic bridge has even attracted scuba divers exploring the underwater landscape, states the Sacramento Bee report.Monticello photographs savedOne of the most striking accounts of the town’s last days came from the photographers Dorothea Lange and Pirkle Jones. The couple spent a year on assignment from Life magazine photographing Monticello and the nearby Berryessa Valley as the residents prepared to move away. Their photographs documented houses, farms, families and landscapes on the verge of extinction. Lange was a celebrated documentary photographer, known especially for her famous photo of Migrant Mother. Jones had been an apprentice of famous landscape photographer Ansel Adams. The photographs came to be known as Death of a Valley. Life never published the full project but excerpts were published in the magazine Aperture in 1960. Decades later, UC Santa Cruz digitized thousands of images from the collection and put them online, letting a new generation see the community that is now under the lake.Painful legacy for former residentsThe loss was more than just the vanishing of buildings for families connected to Monticello. Former residents were dispersed throughout neighboring communities and some could find no affordable farmland to replace what they lost. Families that had lived in the valley for generations suddenly had to re-create their lives somewhere else. It was one chapter in a much larger story of American displacement. Hundreds of communities across the U.S. have been abandoned or submerged due to dam and reservoir projects. Monticello’s experience is a case study of the human costs of infrastructure decisions that can remake entire landscapes while serving populations orders of magnitude larger.Remembering a lost communityThe Monticello Public Cemetery was moved before the reservoir was filled, and is now located near Spanish Flat. With some 600 graves it has become one of the most tangible reminders of the former community. Descendants still gather there, particularly around Memorial Day, connecting families whose hometown disappeared generations ago. The number of surviving residents has steadily declined, making those reunions more and more important. Today Lake Berryessa means recreation, water supply and California’s vast infrastructure network. But behind the front was another story: a town whose houses had been razed, whose valley was flooded and whose residents had been scattered. Monticello might be invisible on the landscape, but its photographs, cemetery, sunken buildings and remaining family memories make sure the community has not totally gone.Images Courtesy: The Sacramento BeeCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.standfirst: El director de MARCA desde 2016 será distinguido el próximo 25 de septiembre en Madrid por Les Valeurs du Monde Unis, dentro de la Cumbre Mundial de los Valores Universales y la jornada dedicada a la Concordia Humanista
articles.summary: El director de MARCA desde 2016 será distinguido el próximo 25 de septiembre en Madrid por Les Valeurs du Monde Unis, dentro de la Cumbre Mundial de los Valores Universales y la jornada dedicada a la Concordia Humanista
articles.body: Juan Ignacio Gallardo, director de MARCA desde marzo de 2016, recibirá el próximo 25 de septiembre en Madrid el Premio al Valor del Periodismo Deportivo Responsable, otorgado por Les Valeurs du Monde Unis. El galardón se entregará dentro de la Cumbre Mundial de los Valores Universales, en la jornada dedicada a la declaración del Día Internacional de la Concordia Humanista. Gallardo se incorporó a MARCA en 1991, tras sus primeras experiencias profesionales en El Informativo de Leganés y Antena 3 Madrid Sur. Desde entonces ha ocupado distintas responsabilidades dentro de la redacción hasta asumir la dirección del periódico, cargo que ejerce desde hace más de nueve años. Unidad Editorial sitúa a MARCA como el diario deportivo de referencia en España, con una audiencia digital de 12,4 millones de usuarios únicos mensuales según los datos de marzo de 2026. El reconocimiento se suma al Premio GLORIA a la Trayectoria en Comunicación Deportiva, recibido por Gallardo en junio de 2025 en el marco del Sports Summit Madrid. En 2026 formó parte además del jurado del Premio Princesa de Asturias de los Deportes. Bajo su dirección, MARCA ha renovado también su colaboración con MADCUP Basket y MADCUP Volley, iniciativas orientadas al desarrollo del deporte base. La Cumbre Mundial de los Valores Universales se celebrará en Madrid los días 24 y 25 de septiembre bajo la presidencia de Su Alteza Real el Emir Lahouari Benarba Ben Mahiedinne Al Hassani. La sede del Comité Olímpico Español acogerá la primera jornada, centrada en el liderazgo, la responsabilidad institucional y la cooperación internacional. La segunda jornada, el 25 de septiembre, incluirá la ceremonia de reconocimientos en la que Gallardo recibirá el premio, junto a otras trayectorias procedentes de la política, la diplomacia, la cultura y la sociedad civil. La iniciativa tiene como una de sus referencias el legado del Emir Abd al-Qadir al-Jaza'iri, recordado por su intervención en Damasco en 1860 para proteger a comunidades amenazadas por la violencia. Con esta distinción, Les Valeurs du Monde Unis reconoce una trayectoria de más de tres décadas en MARCA, desarrollada desde la redacción y consolidada, desde 2016, al frente de uno de los principales medios deportivos en lengua española.

articles.title: 7 dead in Satya Niketan tragedy: Hostel agreement said ‘not responsible’ for casualties or risk
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An alleged PG agreement signed for the very Satya Niketan building that collapsed, killing seven people, stated that the hostel would not b.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An alleged PG agreement signed for the very Satya Niketan building that collapsed, killing seven people, stated that the hostel would not be responsible for any casualties and would not pay compensation for injuries or damage to tenants’ belongings in cases including fire, heavy rain, earthquakes and sealing of the premises, according to a copy of the agreement.The agreement states: “In case of any personal injury suffered / loss / damage of personal belongings of the tenant due to reasons beyond the control of the P.G. vize sealing/fire/earthquake/heavy rains /other natural calamities etc., the hostel will not be liable for paying any compensation.”The document also states: “PG authorities are not responsible for any casualties to tenants.”The clauses in the alleged agreement signed by occupants of the Satya Niketan property have assumed significance following the building collapse and the scrutiny now being faced by PGs operating from residential buildings in the capital.‘Hostel will not be liable for paying compensation’The alleged agreement specifically lists circumstances in which the hostel says it would not be liable for compensation, including sealing, fire, earthquake and heavy rains, as well as other natural calamities.It covers personal injury, loss and damage to tenants' belongings.The document also refers to reasons "beyond the control" of the PG while excluding the hostel from liability in the situations mentioned in the clause.The legal enforceability of such a clause would depend on the facts of the case and applicable law, but the wording of the agreement raises questions about the extent to which responsibility for tenant safety was sought to be excluded through contractual terms.Clause comes under lens after Satya Niketan collapseThe agreement has come to light after the five-storey building housing the PG collapsed in Satya Niketan, near Delhi University's South Campus, leaving seven people dead and several others injured.The collapse has triggered scrutiny of the building's construction, its use as a PG and the role of civic authorities in permitting or monitoring such establishments.Locals had alleged that repair work was being carried out in the basement and that water had accumulated there following days of rain. Civic officials said they could not confirm whether such work was underway until the debris was cleared.The MCD had earlier flagged the collapsed structure as an unauthorised G+4 building in a resettlement colony where permission had been granted only for a G+1 structure.PG safety, accountability under scrutinyThe Satya Niketan tragedy has renewed questions over the safety of private PGs and hostels, particularly those operating from old residential buildings.The Delhi High Court has also expressed concern over the safety of students living in PGs and private hostels and questioned the regulatory framework governing such establishments.The court has directed the MCD to conduct an audit of PGs and hostels and sought details from Delhi University on outstation students and available hostel facilities, noting that inadequate hostel capacity forces many students to depend on private PG accommodation.The agreement from the collapsed Satya Niketan building adds another dimension to the scrutiny — the terms on which students were housed in the property and the extent of responsibility that the operator sought to assume for their safety.The incident has now prompted wider questions over building safety, structural compliance, regulation of PGs and accountability for establishments housing large numbers of students.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Ex-USCIS officer arrested in Texas for allegedly taking cash to approve, fast-track immigration benefits
articles.summary: US News: A former US Citizenship and Immigration Services officer has been arrested in Texas after federal authorities accused him of taking illegal payments i.
articles.body: A former US Citizenship and Immigration Services officer has been arrested in Texas after federal authorities accused him of taking illegal payments in exchange for manipulating immigration decisions and speeding up applications. Lukman Owolabi Ganiyu, a former senior immigration services officer with USCIS, and Adeniyi Akeem Somoye were arrested on September 2 in connection with an alleged multi-year corruption scheme, the US Department of Justice said.A federal criminal complaint filed in the Northern District of Texas on August 31 charges the two men with conspiracy to receive illegal gratuities by a public official.Multi-year scheme by two peopleThe case has put a spotlight on an especially sensitive area of the US immigration system: the alleged sale of access to government officials who have the power to approve or expedite immigration applications.According to federal prosecutors, Ganiyu allegedly used his position as a USCIS officer to manipulate immigration applications, while Somoye allegedly acted as his associate in the scheme.The two are accused of receiving illegal gratuities in return for helping applicants obtain favourable treatment, including unlawful approvals and expedited processing.The Justice Department described the alleged conduct as a “multi-year scheme” and said the investigation involved USCIS' Office of Investigations, the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General and the FBI's Dallas Field Office.“Selling immigration benefits for cash is a blatant abuse of public trust,” US Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould said after the arrests.He added that when a federal official “puts a price tag on lawful status,” authorities would intervene.The FBI also warned that corruption involving immigration decisions can undermine the integrity of a system that has implications for both lawful immigration and national security.“The alleged manipulation of immigration decisions for personal gain undermines the integrity of a process essential to our national security,” FBI Dallas Special Agent in Charge R. Joseph Rothrock said.Why the case mattersUSCIS officers handle a wide range of immigration applications and petitions, including cases involving lawful immigration status and other immigration benefits. Decisions or processing actions by agency officials can therefore have major consequences for applicants waiting to live, work or remain legally in the US.The allegations in the Texas case are particularly significant because they involve the alleged manipulation of that official process from inside the agency.Federal prosecutors have not said in the Justice Department announcement how many applications were allegedly manipulated, how much money the defendants are accused of receiving or how many immigrants may have benefited from the alleged scheme.Those details could emerge as the criminal case progresses.The arrests came amid heightened scrutiny of the US immigration system, with federal authorities pursuing cases involving immigration fraud and abuse from multiple angles. The Northern District of Texas has also recently announced other immigration-related prosecutions, including charges against individuals accused of illegal reentry and previous visa fraud schemes.For Ganiyu, however, the allegation is different: prosecutors say the suspected wrongdoing came from within the federal immigration machinery itself.Both defendants appeared before a US magistrate judge on September 2.If convicted of the conspiracy charge, each faces a maximum sentence of five years in federal prison and a fine of up to $250,000, according to the Justice Department.The case is still at the charging stage. A criminal complaint is an allegation and is not evidence of guilt. Ganiyu and Somoye are presumed innocent unless and until they are proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in court.Assistant US Attorney Chad Meacham from the Fraud Section is prosecuting the case.For immigrants and applicants navigating the US system, the case is likely to serve as another warning about the risks of trying to bypass official procedures through intermediaries or payments.Federal authorities, meanwhile, have made clear that alleged corruption inside the immigration system will be treated as a public-corruption matter rather than simply an immigration violation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari announces crackdown on child marriage after 60,000 underage deliveries
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Monday announced a statewide crackdown on child marriage, ordering house-to-house drives to .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Monday announced a statewide crackdown on child marriage, ordering house-to-house drives to identify underage marriages and pregnancies and warning of arrests, imprisonment and withdrawal of government welfare benefits for those involved.Speaking to the media at Nabanna after a Cabinet meeting, Adhikari said the government would invoke the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 and the POCSO Act against those marrying minors as well as people who facilitate or solemnise such marriages.The announcement came after the state health department reported nearly 60,000 institutional deliveries involving underage girls between January 1 and June 30, according to figures cited by the chief minister.Nearly 60,000 underage deliveries reported in six monthsAdhikari said Murshidabad recorded the highest number, with 12,847 institutional childbirths by underage girls during the six-month period. South 24 Parganas followed with 4,178 cases.He said West Bengal tops the country in child marriages and childbirths involving girls below 18 years of age.The chief minister said every case of pregnancy and childbirth involving a girl below 18 must be reported. The health records would be used by authorities to identify suspected child marriages and initiate action against those responsible.The proposed house-to-house drives will involve coordination between the police, health and social welfare departments and district administrations, with records of underage pregnancies and institutional deliveries being used to identify vulnerable cases.Husbands, facilitators face legal actionAdhikari said husbands of women found to have been married while underage would be issued showcause notices and asked to produce valid proof of their wife's age."If they fail to provide valid proof of the age, strict action will be taken," he said.He warned that police would initiate criminal action and make arrests in cases detected during the crackdown."Police action will be initiated, and arrests will be made," Adhikari said.The government will also withdraw welfare and other scheme benefits from people found to be involved in child marriages, he said.The chief minister issued a warning to priests, qazis and others who solemnise or facilitate underage marriages. Those found involved would face imprisonment and fines under the law.The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act provides for imprisonment of up to two years and/or a fine of up to Rs 1 lakh for people involved in promoting, permitting or conducting a child marriage.Adhikari also said the POCSO Act would be strictly applied, pointing out that sexual relations with a girl below 18 constitute an offence irrespective of whether she is married.He said physical relations with a girl below 18 attract provisions of the POCSO Act, with prison terms ranging from 10 years to life imprisonment and, in certain circumstances, the death penalty.Cases involving pregnancy of minors would attract particularly strict scrutiny and action, he said.Government targets families and those facilitating marriagesThe crackdown will target not only families arranging underage marriages but also husbands, facilitators and those conducting the ceremonies, with authorities expected to use health records to identify suspected cases.The issue has particular significance in West Bengal, where 19th-century social reformer Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar led campaigns against child marriage and for women's education.Adhikari also alleged that the previous Trinamool Congress government had failed to share data on child marriages and underage childbirths with the Centre.The chief minister said the administration would treat cases of child marriage as offences requiring police action and prosecution under the applicable laws.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Shifting right? What AfD's victory in Germany means for Europe, Russia & US
articles.summary: Europe News: Germany has just delivered a political shock that is reverberating far beyond its eastern border.The Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 44.5% of the vo.
articles.body: Germany has just delivered a political shock that is reverberating far beyond its eastern border.The Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 44.5% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, more than doubling its 2021 tally and crushing Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats, which fell to 18.5%. The result was historic as no far-right party has come this close to dominating a German state since World War 2.The immediate political effect may be limited as mainstream German parties still refuse to cooperate with the AfD, but the psychological effect is already being felt.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Germany’s political firewall against the far right has been breached electorally, and the question now spreading across the continent and the world is simple: is Europe turning right?The answer increasingly appears to be yes. So, what does it mean for the European Union, Nato, Russia and the US?Germany's warning shotAfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund's triumph is particularly significant because Germany has long been the country where the political barrier against the far right was considered strongest given its history.That barrier remains institutionally intact. But electorally, it is under extraordinary pressure.As per political analysts, the party's success reflects a combination of anger over immigration, economic frustration, dissatisfaction with mainstream parties and opposition to Berlin's support for Ukraine. Its rise also demonstrates that the AfD is no longer simply a protest vehicle for voters on Germany's political fringes.Germany is also Europe's economic and political heavyweight.If the AfD eventually becomes part of a future federal government, its positions on Russia, Ukraine, Nato and the EU could become questions for the entire continent.For now, however, Germany is more likely to see a different effect: the mainstream right moving further right to stop voters from defecting to the AfD.That is how Europe's political centre can shift even while the far right remains outside government.France could be the next big testMarine Le Pen's National Rally has spent years transforming itself from a party of protest into a plausible governing force. Whether Le Pen herself is ultimately able to contest the 2027 presidential election remains a legal and political question, but the RN's position is clear: it is now a serious contender for power.Recent polling has placed an RN candidate, Le Pen or Jordan Bardella, at roughly one-third of the first-round vote, substantially ahead of individual mainstream challengers.In several second-round scenarios, Bardella has also been competitive or ahead.France is crucial because a right-wing government there would not merely alter immigration policy.France is a nuclear power, a permanent member of the UN Security Council, one of Nato's most important militaries and the EU's other major strategic power alongside Germany.A National Rally government could therefore reshape debates over European defence, Ukraine, sanctions against Russia and the future of the EU.The party has moderated some of its earlier positions on Russia, but the issue remains contentious. Current RN figures have argued for continued support for Ukraine while demanding a fundamentally different relationship between French assistance and national interests.Right = Pro-Putin? Meloni says noItalian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and her right-wing administration has surpassed 1,413 consecutive days in office, making her government the longest-serving uninterrupted single-term administration in Italy since World War 2.Despite Meloni's marathon tenure, Italy remains firmly within the Nato camp.Her Brothers of Italy remains the country's largest party, polling around 25-26%, while a new and more radical force led by former general Roberto Vannacci has risen rapidly. Reuters reported in September that Vannacci's party had overtaken Silvio Berlusconi's Forza Italia in polling.Meloni's continued success is important as it complicates the idea that a rightward Europe necessarily means a pro-Russian Europe.She has taken a hard line on immigration and embraced socially conservative politics, but she has also backed Ukraine, maintained close ties with Washington and accepted Italy's role within Nato.The danger for her now comes from her right.If Vannacci's movement continues to grow, Meloni could face pressure to adopt a more nationalist and confrontational position towards Brussels and a less hawkish approach towards Moscow.Italy therefore offers Europe a choice between two versions of the right: Meloni's conservative Atlanticism or a more radical nationalist model.Spain could make the far right kingmakerThe conservative People's Party is leading national polling at around 32%, with the governing Socialists at approximately 26%. Vox, meanwhile, is hovering around 18%, up significantly from its 2023 election performance.That makes Vox potentially decisive.Recent regional elections have already shown the pattern: the PP can win, but may need Vox to govern. In Andalusia, for example, the PP won the election but lost its absolute majority, leaving Vox with significant leverage.Vox leader Santiago Abascal has welcomed the AfD's success.The significance is not necessarily that Vox will take power by itself. It is that the radical right may become impossible for Europe's mainstream conservatives to ignore.The far right does not have to win outright to win influence. It only has to become indispensable.Poland: The right is rising, but Putin is a problemPoland presents perhaps the biggest obstacle to the idea of a unified European right.The country's conservative and nationalist parties remain powerful. But Polish politics is shaped by a fundamental reality that does not apply with the same intensity elsewhere: Russia is viewed as an existential security threat.Recent polling shows the ruling Civic Coalition around 31%, Law and Justice around 22%, the Confederation around 14-15% and the more radical Confederation of the Polish Crown near 10%.The combined strength of the right is therefore enormous.But its Russia policy can be very different from the AfD's.That explains Prime Minister Donald Tusk's furious reaction to Germans celebrating the AfD victory. He described those celebrating the result as "idiots or traitors".Poland demonstrates why the phrase "Europe's right" can be misleading.There is no single European right.There are nationalists who want to weaken Brussels but strengthen Nato. There are conservatives who want tougher immigration policies while remaining strongly pro-Ukraine. And there are parties that question sanctions against Moscow and want a fundamental reset with Russia.Those differences could determine Europe's future.What does all this mean for Putin?For Russia, the best possible outcome is not necessarily a Europe full of openly pro-Russian governments.It is a divided Europe.The EU's ability to impose sanctions, finance Ukraine and coordinate economic pressure on Moscow depends on political consensus. Nato's deterrence depends on member states agreeing on the nature of the Russian threat.If France, Germany, Italy, Spain and Poland begin adopting substantially different positions on Ukraine and Russia, Europe's collective leverage could weaken even if every individual country remains formally inside Nato.But there is an important counterargument.A rightward Europe could also become more militarily capable.Meloni's Italy, Poland's conservatives and Europe's mainstream centre-right increasingly support higher defence spending and stronger national militaries. A Europe that is more conservative on immigration and more nationalist about sovereignty could still become more determined to defend itself against Russia.Trump gets his European political momentThe AfD victory also matters enormously for Donald Trump.Trump has repeatedly backed Europe's nationalist right and criticised European political establishments over immigration, national sovereignty and their approach to Russia and Ukraine.The AfD's breakthrough gives Trump's movement a powerful argument: Europe's voters are moving in the direction he has been advocating.For Trump, the result is therefore politically useful.It provides evidence that the European establishment is losing voters to parties promising tougher immigration controls, greater national sovereignty and a rejection of the old political consensus.But there is a contradiction.Trump wants Europe to become more responsible for its own defence. A nationalist Europe could spend more on defence and reduce its dependence on Washington.Yet if nationalism also produces divisions over Ukraine, Russia and Nato, America could end up with a Europe that is more willing to spend but less willing to act together.That is not necessarily what Washington wants.Europe is not turning right in one directionThe AfD victory should therefore not be read as proof that Europe is about to become a continent of far-right governments.The more profound change may be happening inside mainstream parties.Conservatives are adopting tougher positions on immigration. Defence spending is rising. National sovereignty has returned to the centre of political debate.Mainstream parties are increasingly forced to compete with nationalist movements on their own terrain.That could produce a Europe that is more conservative without becoming uniformly far-right.If the European right follows Meloni's model, Europe could become tougher on migration, more assertive about national interests and simultaneously committed to Nato and Ukraine.If it follows the AfD's model, the EU's unity on Russia could come under severe strain.If France moves towards the RN while Germany moves towards the AfD, and Spain's Vox becomes indispensable to government formation, Europe's political centre of gravity could shift dramatically.But Poland could remain firmly anti-Russian, while Italy remains Atlanticist under Meloni.That is why the next chapter of European politics will not simply be about left versus right.It will be about which right wins, and what it believes Europe should do about Russia, America and the EU itself.The AfD's victory has shown that the old political order is under pressure.The elections and political battles now unfolding across Europe will determine whether that pressure produces a new conservative mainstream, or a fractured continent where Moscow finds more room to manoeuvre.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Greta Ramirez-Guerrero: The Canadian PhD student who helped reveal a 450-million-year-old jellyfish relative hiding in Quebec rocks
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Greta Ramirez-Guerrero was studying fragments of ancient life that had survived in Quebec rock for roughly 450 million years when she encountered an u.
articles.body: Greta Ramirez-Guerrero was studying fragments of ancient life that had survived in Quebec rock for roughly 450 million years when she encountered an unusual problem: the animal she was examining had almost nothing that should have fossilised well. Paleocanna tentaculum was a soft-bodied relative of modern jellyfish, shaped more like a narrow tube than the drifting creatures familiar from today's seas. Yet dozens of its delicate remains had endured in limestone from the Ordovician period. Ramirez-Guerrero, a PhD candidate at the Université de Montréal, led the study that pieced together what the fossils represented.Across 15 slabs, the team identified around 135 specimens, giving her an unusually large collection of evidence for an animal of this kind. Their arrangement in the rock also offered clues about how quickly the creatures were buried and how their soft bodies managed to leave a trace behind.Greta Ramirez-Guerrero identified a 450-million-year-old jellyfish relativeThe fossils did not resemble the image most people have of a jellyfish. Paleocanna tentaculum was a polyp, with an elongated body enclosed within a narrow tube. At one end was a ring of tentacles.That distinction mattered to Ramirez-Guerrero's work because soft-bodied organisms are notoriously difficult to preserve. Once an animal dies, its tissues can disappear quickly, leaving little behind for future palaeontologists to find.Yet these specimens had survived as carbonaceous impressions in the Upper Ordovician Neuville Formation of Quebec. The study, published in the Journal of Paleontology in February 2026, described the fossils as a new genus and species of medusozoan.For Ramirez-Guerrero, the task was therefore not simply recognising an unusual shape in a rock. She had to work out what the animal was, where it belonged among ancient relatives and what its preservation could reveal about the circumstances in which it had been buried.135 fossils gave Greta a rare chance to trace its ancient lineageAccording to Discover Magazine, the material gave her a reasonable amount to work with, even if the fossils themselves were delicate. Around 135 Paleocanna individuals were spread across 15 slabs of shaly limestone.39 specimens were measured and photographed in detail. Their physical characteristics were then compared with 69 fossil and living species related to jellyfish. A fossil can resemble several different organisms when only part of its anatomy has survived, so Ramirez-Guerrero and her co-authors used a much wider set of morphological features to establish its position.Their analysis placed Paleocanna tentaculum as an early-branching member of the crown group Medusozoa. The results indicated that it was more closely related to the group containing modern cubozoans, scyphozoans and staurozoans than to some other fossil medusozoans.Greta found clues in the way the fossils were arrangedSome of the most useful information was not simply in the shape of the individual animals. It was in their arrangement.Several specimens were aligned in the same direction. Others occurred in small clusters, with two or three tubes attached near their bases. Ramirez-Guerrero interpreted the alignment as evidence that the animals had probably been buried where they lived, or had moved very little before burial.That observation helped reconstruct what happened at the seafloor hundreds of millions of years ago. Fine sediment appears to have covered the organisms rapidly. Conditions around the buried animals were also relatively low in oxygen, slowing the decay of their soft bodies before the sediment eventually hardened into rock.It was an unusual chain of events. Without it, there may have been nothing for Ramirez-Guerrero to study.A 2010 fossil find eventually led Greta to a new speciesAccording to the Université de Montréal, Ramirez-Guerrero did not discover the fossils in the field herself. They had been collected in 2010 by John Iellamo, an amateur fossil collector and member of the Musée de paléontologie et de l'évolution in Montreal. He recognised that the specimens were scientifically important and donated them to the museum.Years later, that material became the basis for Ramirez-Guerrero's study. The scientific description established the Paleocanna tentaculum as both a new genus and a new species. The name refers to the animal's ancient, tube-like form, while the species description reflects its tentacles.The physical measurements also give an idea of its proportions. The fossils analysed in the study had an average length of about 36.9 millimetres and an average width of around 6 millimetres, although individual specimens varied.For an animal that lived in the Ordovician seas, those measurements might seem like a small detail. They become more useful when combined with the tube structure, tentacle arrangement, surface markings and relationship to other medusozoans.Together, they allow palaeontologists to distinguish the species from other ancient organisms that occupied similar marine environments.Greta's study adds another piece to the ancient jellyfish family treeJellyfish and their relatives have an extremely old evolutionary history, but their fossil record is patchy. The problem is partly biological: animals made mostly of soft tissue are much less likely to leave recognisable fossils than organisms protected by shells or other hard structures.That makes Ramirez-Guerrero's study useful beyond the naming of one species. Paleocanna tentaculum provides another anatomical point of comparison for scientists trying to understand how medusozoans changed through deep time. Its position in the evolutionary analysis suggests that some of the features associated with the modern jellyfish lineage have roots extending into the Ordovician.The fossil does not fill every gap. It does, however, give researchers another well-preserved organism to work with.The site may offer Ramirez-Guerrero more fossils to studyThe fossils came from Saint-Joachim in the Saint Lawrence Lowlands, a locality known for its rich Ordovician record. The researchers examined only the material available on the 15 slabs used in their study.That leaves plenty of room for further work, particularly because fossil sites of this kind can continue producing specimens after an unusual organism has first been recognised.The existing fossils are now curated at the Musée de paléontologie et de l'évolution in Montreal. For Ramirez-Guerrero, they represent more than a new name in an old rock. They provide a rare opportunity to examine a soft-bodied member of an ancient lineage and to work out how an animal that vanished hundreds of millions of years ago fits into the evolutionary history of jellyfish and their relatives.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
