articles.title: A 3,000-year-old ship-shaped stone grave was discovered in Sweden; four urns inside contained burnt human bones and a metal object
articles.summary: Europe News: Archaeologists discovered a prehistoric burial site near Domsten, north of Helsingborg, while monitoring work to replace the Öresund cables. The disco.
articles.body: Archaeologists discovered a prehistoric burial site near Domsten, north of Helsingborg, while monitoring work to replace the Öresund cables. The discovery includes a stone structure shaped like a small ship, measuring about three metres long, as well as two circular stone structures. Four burial urns were also recovered from the site. X-ray images later showed burnt bones and a metal object in one of them. As per Sweden’s national transmission system operator (Svenska kraftnät), they are around 2,500 to 3,000 years old, which places them in the earlier Bronze Age or the early Pre-Roman Iron Age. Archaeologists discovered the site while monitoring work in an area where earlier graves had also been found. Further examination is planned for the autumn that could provide new clues about the people buried there.Ancient ship-shaped stone grave discovered near DomstenThe discovery was made during archaeological monitoring carried out in connection with Svenska kraftnät’s work on the Öresund cables. Archaeologists initially uncovered flint remains linked to older settlements. They later discovered a stone structure hidden beneath what appeared to be an ordinary stone mound. The structure consisted of a small, ship-shaped stone setting measuring around three metres in length. Two circular stone structures were also found alongside it. Archaeologists believe the site may originally have been covered with earth or peat, creating a low burial mound.How archaeologists estimated the age of the ancient remainsThe human remains have not yet undergone a full analysis, so archaeologists have estimated their age from the form and construction of the graves. The burial structures suggest that they belong to the earlier part of the Bronze Age or the transition to the Pre-Roman Iron Age, which places the remains roughly 2,500 to 3,000 years old.The discovery also adds to the archaeological evidence from the surrounding area. A separate group of graves found nearby in 2019 was dated to approximately 1400 to 1050 BC. The two discoveries are located around 100 metres apart.X-rays reveal burnt bones inside four ancient burial urnsFour burial urns were recovered during the excavation. The vessels were described as very well preserved and were almost completely intact when archaeologists removed them from the site. Their condition made it possible to remove all four as a whole for further examination. The urns were subsequently examined using X-rays. The images revealed burnt bones inside the vessels, along with a metal object in one of them. The findings indicate that the urns contain material that can now be studied in greater detail.What could further examination reveal about the Domsten gravesReportedly, archaeologists will examine the recovered material in greater detail, including the burial urns and their contents. The preserved bones may provide information about the people buried at the site, including estimates of their age and sex. Researchers will also examine the metal object identified by the X-rays and look for other possible grave goods. The discovery has also raised questions about the wider burial landscape around Domsten.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Celia Hunter flew a war-surplus plane to Alaska in 1947 and built a wilderness life near Denali; 54 years later, at 82, her final night was spent fighting to protect the Arctic Refuge
articles.summary: US News: Celia Hunter spent the final evening of her life writing urgent letters to US politicians, asking them to oppose oil drilling in the Arctic National W.
articles.body: Celia Hunter spent the final evening of her life writing urgent letters to US politicians, asking them to oppose oil drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. It brought an end to a 54-year campaign to protect Alaska's wild landscapes. According to historical records documented by the Alaska Conservation Foundation, Hunter died in her sleep on 1 December 2001 at the age of 82. Her death marked the end of an environmental career that began when she flew surplus military aircraft north to Fairbanks in the winter of 1946. Hunter co-founded the Alaska Conservation Society in 1960 and later helped establish the Alaska Conservation Foundation in 1980. Over more than five decades, her work helped protect more than 100 million acres of public land across Alaska.Military service and the northern flightBorn in Arlington, Washington, in 1919 and raised in a Quaker family, Hunter learned to fly in 1940. During the Second World War, she joined the Women Airforce Service Pilots (WASP), flying military aircraft from factories to supply bases across the continental United States. Federal rules did not allow female pilots to fly military aircraft through Canada to Alaska, but Hunter remained determined to visit the territory. In late 1946, Hunter and fellow WASP pilot Ginny Hill Wood made an agreement with an Alaskan pilot in Seattle to deliver two war-surplus aircraft to Fairbanks. They took off in early December, and the winter journey lasted 27 days in difficult weather. Recalling the flight in archival material kept by the Alaska Conservation Foundation, Hunter described the harsh conditions. “It took us 27 days to fly from Seattle to Fairbanks. Ginny's plane had unairworthy fabric and no heat—we nicknamed it 'Li'l Igloo'. On the leg between Watson Lake and Whitehorse, a three-hour flight, we had to chip her out of the cockpit when we landed; she was so cold she couldn't move!” Hunter remarked. When the two women reached Fairbanks on 1 January 1947, sub-zero temperatures had stopped commercial flights. They were forced to stay and found work as flight attendants on early commercial flights to Nome and Kotzebue.Wilderness tourism at Camp DenaliWhen Hunter first arrived in Alaska, she did not see herself as a conservation campaigner. “I don't think 'conservationist' existed in my vocabulary at that time. We were just looking for adventures!” Hunter later noted. After briefly studying in Sweden and travelling through post-war Europe, Hunter and Wood returned to Alaska. In 1951, they joined Wood's husband in claiming a homestead under the Homestead Act near the boundary of what was then Mount McKinley National Park. A year later, in 1952, they established Camp Denali, a wilderness lodge based on the European hut system. It offered simple accommodation while also teaching visitors about nature. Their approach set strict environmental standards for tourism at the time. “We specialized in providing healthy, sustaining meals, with fresh baked bread and pastries, and we refused to handle either soft drinks or beer in our small store because we didn't want to see the throw-away cans littering the roadsides,” Hunter recalled. They ran Camp Denali until 1975, when they sold the property. The lodge was later included within the expanded boundaries of Denali National Park and Preserve.Organizing the Alaska conservation movementAs industrial development, resource extraction and military projects grew across Alaska after the war, Hunter turned towards organised environmental campaigning. Having seen Alaska's huge wilderness areas before statehood, Hunter remembered how connected and untouched the landscape appeared. “Flying across bush Alaska, the entire landscape was a seamless whole, unmarred by man-made boundaries,” Hunter observed. In 1960, Hunter and her colleagues created the Alaska Conservation Society, the first statewide volunteer environmental group in Alaska. The organisation gave local residents a way to speak on federal conservation policies, including plans to establish the Arctic National Wildlife Range. In 1976, Hunter became the first woman to serve as interim executive director of The Wilderness Society. She led national campaigns during an important period of debate over federal land policy. In 1980, she co-founded the Alaska Conservation Foundation, which provided grants and financial support to grassroots environmental groups across the state. Her work received major recognition. In 1991, the Sierra Club gave Hunter the John Muir Award, its highest honour for lifetime conservation work. The Wilderness Society followed with the Robert Marshall Award in 1998. Hunter continued taking part in public policy debates into her eighties. She regularly wrote to federal officials and mentored younger conservationists. On the night she died in December 2001, she stayed late at her desk writing letters to members of the US Congress, urging them to vote against allowing petroleum exploration on the coastal plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity
articles.summary: The PSNI described the scam as "sophisticated" and said the victim was encouraged to borrow money to continue investing.
articles.body:
A person has lost £250,000 after falling victim to an AI-generated scam.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said the victim saw what appeared to be an AI-generated video featuring a well-known personality from the financial sector.

The advertisement promoted an investment opportunity and claimed significant returns.

A spokesperson for the PSNI said an "apparent celebrity endorsement" should never be regarded as proof that an investment is genuine.

The PSNI did not confirm who the celebrity was who was used in the AI-generated video, but BBC News NI has seen scams online using financial experts such as Martin Lewis, Peter Jones and Steven Bartlett.

After initially investing a relatively small amount, the victim was contacted through WhatsApp and encouraged to make further payments.

Police said the fraudsters persuaded the victim in the Ards and north Down area to create multiple online accounts and gained remote access to their computer, claiming they were helping with the investment.

The PSNI described the scam as "sophisticated" and said the victim was encouraged to borrow money to continue investing, with funds transferred to accounts controlled by the criminals.

A spokesperson for the PSNI said the criminals gradually gained the victim's trust before encouraging increasingly significant payments.

They added that fraudsters could create "extremely convincing" advertisements, websites and communications, with artificial intelligence also being used to fabricate videos, voices and apparent endorsements.

Superintendent Joanne Gibson, chair of the Scamwise Partnership, urged people to "stop and check" financial activity and encouraged families to talk to relatives about fraud.

Police have advised people to independently verify who they are dealing with and, where appropriate, check that anyone offering financial services is authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority.

articles.title: India, China hold first corps commander talks in Arunachal Pradesh’s eastern sector
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The Indian and Chinese armies reviewed the situation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in the Arunachal Pradesh sector during corps co.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Indian and Chinese armies reviewed the situation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in the Arunachal Pradesh sector during corps commander-level talks on Sunday, days after the two countries held Special Representative (SR) talks in Beijing on the long-standing boundary question.The meeting was held at the Wacha-Damai border meeting point in Arunachal Pradesh's Kibithoo region, with the focus on maintaining peace and tranquillity along the frontier, people familiar with the matter said, as per news agency PTI.The Indian delegation was headed by Lieutenant General Girish Kalia, commander of the Indian Army's Dimapur-based 3 Corps. There was no official word on the talks.The meeting came amid reports of aggressive military posturing by Chinese troops along the LAC in the Upper Subansiri region of Arunachal Pradesh.First corps commander-level talks in eastern sectorThe latest engagement was the first corps commander-level military meeting between the two sides at the Wacha-Damai border meeting point.India and China have primarily held such military-level meetings at the Chusul-Moldo border meeting point in the Ladakh sector.The latest engagement provided a mechanism for the two sides to address issues in the eastern sector through military channels.The Indian Army has two Corps formations looking after the LAC in Arunachal Pradesh — the Tezpur-based 4 Corps and the Rangapahar-based 3 Corps. The 3 Corps is responsible for operational areas along the LAC in Arunachal Pradesh.India and China have different perceptions of the LAC, which have at times resulted in face-offs.Talks follow Doval-Wang meeting in BeijingThe corps commander-level meeting came days after national security adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi held the SR talks in Beijing on August 25.The discussions focused on delimitation of the frontier and sustaining work on trans-boundary cooperation. India conveyed the importance of maintaining peace and tranquillity along the frontier for the overall development of bilateral ties.In his remarks at the meeting, Doval said normalcy in India-China relations had been a direct result of both sides maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas.The ministry of external affairs had said the Indian side highlighted the importance of maintaining peace and tranquillity in the India-China border areas for the continued development and progress of bilateral relations.Doval and Wang are the designated Special Representatives for the boundary talks mechanism, which was established in 2003 to comprehensively address the dispute over the 3,488-km India-China border.Eight-point consensus on border managementThe SR talks resulted in an eight-point consensus aimed at improving management of the border.The two sides agreed to advance consultations for an "early and substantial harvest" of boundary delimitation and directed the Expert Group on Boundary Delimitation and Working Group on Border Management to take forward discussions.They also agreed to set up two additional meeting points for military talks and two more channels of border military hotlines in the Eastern and Middle sectors.The two sides agreed that situations on the ground would be addressed promptly through existing diplomatic and military channels, including the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs, local commander-level meetings and other agreed mechanisms.The joint statement said the two sides discussed ways to improve their understanding of the LAC in appropriate areas for better border management.The two countries also reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas and creating an atmosphere for the healthy and steady development of bilateral relations.The consensus also covered trans-border trade and cooperation on rivers. Both sides agreed to strengthen exchanges and cooperation in border trade, pilgrimage and other areas.They also agreed to hold the next meeting of the India-China Expert-Level Mechanism on Trans-border Rivers in September.Efforts to rebuild bilateral tiesThe latest military engagement comes as India and China have taken a series of measures in recent months to rebuild their relationship after ties came under severe strain following the deadly Galwan Valley clashes in 2020.The two sides also agreed to hold the 26th round of Special Representative talks in India in 2027.

articles.title: A Texas family held this coastal ranch for generations; now 2,500 acres have become part of a 17,500-acre wildlife refuge
articles.summary: US News: For generations, the Ward family knew a stretch of the Texas coast as “Down Below,” a working ranch where cattle grazing, hunting and family tradition.
articles.body: For generations, the Ward family knew a stretch of the Texas coast as “Down Below,” a working ranch where cattle grazing, hunting and family traditions unfolded across prairie, wetlands and marshes. Now, 2,500 acres of that land have entered a very different chapter. The property has been permanently protected and added to the Justin Hurst Wildlife Management Area near Freeport, creating more than 17,500 acres of connected conserved habitat in Brazoria County. The deal brought together the Ward family, the Coastal Prairie Conservancy and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, turning land that had been privately stewarded for generations into part of a much larger conservation landscape.A family ranch with roots stretching back generationsThe newly protected property was not simply another parcel of undeveloped Texas land. Known within the Ward family as “Down Below”, it had been owned and cared for by generations of the family, whose Texas roots reach back to Emily Austin Perry, the sister of Stephen F. Austin. Her descendants were among the settlers associated with Austin’s “Old Three Hundred”, linking the property to a much longer history of ranching and settlement along the Texas coast. Over the decades, the Wards maintained the landscape as a working ranch while also managing it for wildlife. Lee Taylor Ward, a lifelong rancher and outdoorsman, was particularly devoted to the property. His family said he believed the land mattered not only to them, but also to wildlife, ranching and the future of the Texas coast.The 2,500-acre tract is now part of a much larger habitatThe conservation deal adds 2,500 acres immediately west and north of the existing Justin Hurst Wildlife Management Area. Before the expansion, the wildlife management area covered roughly 15,033 acres; the addition brings the connected protected landscape to more than 17,500 acres. The property contains a mixture of coastal prairie, wetlands and tidal marsh, habitats that are increasingly valuable along a heavily developed stretch of the Texas Gulf Coast. According to the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, the wider area provides habitat for species including Black Rails and Mottled Ducks, alongside migratory waterfowl, shorebirds and other coastal wildlife. Protecting the Ward property also strengthens the connection between existing conserved lands, including the nearby San Bernard National Wildlife Refuge, creating a larger and more continuous landscape for wildlife.The family’s traditional land management will continueAlthough ownership has changed, the land will not simply be left untouched. The Texas Parks and Wildlife Department plans to continue many of the management practices the Ward family used over the years, including cattle grazing, prescribed burning and regulated hunting. Those activities can play an important role in maintaining the character of coastal prairie and other habitats when they are carefully managed. The Ward family’s approach had already combined ranching with stewardship, helping preserve the ecological qualities of the property while keeping it a working landscape. The acquisition therefore represents less of a complete change in how the land is treated and more of a permanent commitment to maintaining it for wildlife and future generations. TPWD said the property will eventually be incorporated into the broader public-access framework of the Justin Hurst Wildlife Management Area.A family legacy becomes a permanent part of Texas conservationThe acquisition was made possible through funding from a RESTORE Act grant, which directs money connected to the Deepwater Horizon oil spill towards restoration and protection projects along the Gulf Coast. Additional support came through the Partnership for Gulf Coast Land Conservation and the Galveston Bay Estuary Program Conservation Assistance Program. For the Ward family, however, the significance reaches beyond funding or acreage. Permanently protecting “Down Below” ensures that a landscape associated with generations of family memories will remain intact even as development pressure continues along the Texas coast. Emily Ward said her late husband, Lee Taylor Ward, loved the property and believed its importance extended beyond the family. Now, the 2,500-acre ranch will form part of a 17,500-acre protected landscape where coastal prairie, wetlands and marshes can continue supporting wildlife long into the future.The expansion is another example of how private land can become an important part of large-scale conservation. Rather than isolating protected areas, the project connects another substantial tract of coastal habitat to the existing Justin Hurst Wildlife Management Area and nearby conserved lands. That continuity matters for wildlife living across wetlands, prairie and marsh, particularly along a Gulf Coast facing increasing development and environmental pressures. For the Ward family, the decision also gives a centuries-old connection to the Texas landscape a lasting future. The ranch may no longer belong to the family, but the way they cared for it will continue to influence its management. What was once known simply as “Down Below” is now part of one of the Texas coast’s largest connected protected landscapes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Man 'planned paint protest at Boris Johnson wedding party', court hears
articles.summary: A court hears Tim Speers, from Cornwall, planned to write the word "Palestine" on the venue's lawn.
articles.body:
An alleged activist planned to spray the word "Palestine" on a lawn at Boris Johnson's wedding party venue, a court has heard.

Jurors at Southwark Crown Court were told police approached Tim Speers, 41, at a Cotswold estate as they thought he looked "quite out of place". The former prime minister was due to celebrate his marriage to Carrie Johnson at the Gloucestershire site the following day.

During the opening of Speers' trial, the jury was told police found Speers and another man - who is due to face trial at a later date - were carrying spray paint and super glue.

Speers, of Fairfield Road in Bude, Cornwall, denies having items with intent to damage property. The trial continues.

Jurors were told Speers and the man were stopped with cans of beers at the Daylesford Estate - which belongs to Conservative Party donor Lord Anthony Bamford - on 29 July 2022.

They initially refused to tell police why they were there and then said they were on holiday, the jury heard.

Prosecutor Christiaan Moll told the court a voice note recorded by Speers the day before his arrest was found by police, in which he said he had been asked by two people from Palestine Action to take part in "action", which he had "agreed to do".

Jurors were told Speers said in the voice message: "There's this big heart mowed into his lawn, so the idea is to just go up to it and write Palestine in red paint, through a weed sprayer."

Moll said the voice note added: "So basically that Lord Bamford is hosting some like party this weekend, Boris Johnson.

"Lord Bamford is like the owner, his family the owner of JCB if no-one's aware… the Israeli government basically use JCBs to bulldoze Palestinian homes to create way for Israeli settlers, so this dude just profits from untold suffering."

The prosecution said Speers was expected to accept he had the paint and glue, as well as making the voice note, but would likely say he had abandoned the planned protest after arriving at the estate and noticing the large security presence.

The Johnsons were married in a private ceremony at Westminster Cathedral in May 2021. They hosted their wedding celebrations at Daylesford House on 30 July the following year, setting up marquees and hay bales in the grounds.

articles.title: Claimed Israeli capture of Lebanese ridge reshapes negotiation dynamics
articles.summary: Israel’s continued strikes challenge Lebanon’s push for an elusive peace agreement and stability.
articles.body:
Israel claims operational control over Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, potentially impacting negotiations with Lebanese government later this month.

Israeli military operation to seize ridge ongoing for weeks, citing presence of Hezbollah tunnels, underground operations rooms, and living quarters for fighters.

Despite ceasefire agreement, Israel continues military operations in Lebanon, raising questions about future of negotiations with Hezbollah.

Beirut, Lebanon – On Friday, Israel claimed to have established operational control over the Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, a development in its fight against Hezbollah that analysts believe could also give Israel greater leverage in negotiations with the Lebanese government planned for later this month.

The Israeli operation to seize the ridge has been ongoing for weeks – and what it says are Hezbollah tunnels underneath – with frequent drone and air strikes by the Israeli military. Analysts told Al Jazeera that the strategically important high ground is significant for the Israelis and Hezbollah because it overlooks a number of nearby regions, including the southern city of Nabatieh.

As well as its claims about a network of Hezbollah tunnels, Israel also says the Iranian-backed Lebanese group had underground operations rooms, weapons stores and living quarters for fighters. Despite Israel's assertion that it has control over the ridge, military operations and attacks are reportedly ongoing.

That is despite the June "ceasefire" Israel agreed with Lebanon, but which is being repeatedly violated.

Political and security analyst, Bassel Doueik, told Al Jazeera that Ali al-Taher is crucial to the outcome of Lebanese-Israeli negotiations.

"Israel has continued to breach the ceasefire daily and the Lebanese government is still trying to negotiate because it doesn't have any other choice," Doueik said. "However, if Israel actually occupies the hill, it will give it more of an upper hand in the negotiations because it will be occupying more land."

Israel and Lebanon began engaging in US-mediated direct negotiations in April, despite Hezbollah's opposition.

The talks come after nearly three years of Israeli attacks on Lebanon. The latest war began on October 8, 2023, when Hezbollah attacked Israel after the beginning of its genocidal war on Gaza. Israel then unilaterally intensified fighting in September 2024, eventually killing more than 4,000 people in Lebanon and assassinating much of Hezbollah's military leadership, including longtime Secretary-General, Hassan Nasrallah. It also invaded southern Lebanon and began demolishing homes and infrastructure throughout the area.

A ceasefire was agreed in November 2024 but Israel violated the agreement more than 10,000 times. Hezbollah resumed its attacks in response to this year's US-Israeli war with Iran.

Israel responded by re-invading Lebanon and launching attacks across the country, including killing more than 350 people in what became known as Black Wednesday . In late June, a framework agreement was announced between Tel Aviv and Beirut aimed at ending the fighting in Lebanon, launching so-called "pilot zones" where the Lebanese Army would disarm Hezbollah.

Despite the agreement and ongoing negotiations, Israeli forces never stopped attacking Lebanon. Beirut says it continues talks because it is the only option it has.

Israel now says the framework agreement is failing, even if the Lebanese government doesn't want to give up on it just yet.

"The Lebanese are pushing for pilot zones in areas where the Israelis are currently operating, so they can pull back their troops, but Israel is more interested in pilot zones in areas it is not operating," Nicholas Blanford, a non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and author of a book about Hezbollah, told Al Jazeera.

He added that few in Lebanon appear optimistic about the pilot zone plan.

In recent weeks, Israel has focused many of its attacks on the Qantara mountain range and the Ali al-Taher ridge, where Hezbollah fighters are reported to be.

On Sunday, the Israeli military killed seven people in the southern villages of Arab Salim and Nabatieh al-Fawqa. On Monday, 12 people were killed in Israeli attacks in Kfar Rumman.

Analysts said the ridge has geographic importance to both Hezbollah and Israel.

"The location is of strategic importance to Hezbollah," Blanford said. "It has dominating views looking west over Nabatieh, dominating views over east over Marjayoun and Khiam to Shebaa, and part of [the occupied] Golan Heights in northern Israel looking south, so it is a strategic area and entirely credible that [Hezbollah] has a massive bunker complex within that hill."

However, Blanford does not expect the Israelis to attempt to hold Ali al-Taher.

"If the Israelis wanted to keep Ali al-Taher, they would have to seize the high ground to the north and northeast because otherwise it would be vulnerable to attacks by Hezbollah," he said, recalling a similar dynamic during the Israelis' 18-year occupation of south Lebanon from 1982-2000. "I'm not sure the Israelis would want to extend that deep, so they would likely dynamite it and pull back their forces to more defensible ground."

Hezbollah continues to oppose direct negotiations with Israeli leaders. It has previously said it prefers indirect talks, similar to how the 2024 ceasefire was arranged.

"The negotiations seemed to have reached an impasse because Lebanon and Israel fundamentally disagree on the implementation of the pilot zones scheme," David Wood, the International Crisis Group's senior analyst for Lebanon, told Al Jazeera. "Lebanon argues that Israel has not withdrawn from any areas that it directly occupied, while Israel insists that it will not withdraw until Hezbollah disarms."

The question now is whether the Israeli advance in Ali al-Taher will give them even more leverage over Lebanon in talks set to resume later this month.

Doueik said that talks were unlikely to change the status quo on the ground, with the Israeli government focused on projecting an image of strength ahead of elections next month.

"The most crucial point in the Lebanese-Israeli negotiations is the upcoming October elections," he said.

articles.title: Alice Weidel: The Banker Behind the Firewall
articles.summary: Europe News: Since Sunday night in Magdeburg, when the Alternative für Deutschland took 43.9 per cent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt against 17.2 for a Christian Dem.
articles.body: Since Sunday night in Magdeburg, when the Alternative für Deutschland took 43.9 per cent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt against 17.2 for a Christian Democratic Union that had run the state for a quarter of a century, the question Germans have spent a decade avoiding has acquired a date and a number. The woman at the centre of it, and the reason a great many Germans find her difficult to place, is Alice Weidel.Consider the biography before the politics, because the biography is the politics. Weidel was born in Gütersloh in 1979, read business and economics at Bayreuth, wrote a doctorate on China's pension system, worked for the Bank of China and spent six years in the country. She admires Margaret Thatcher, chiefly for the stubbornness. Her economics are the ordinary furniture of the free-market right: lower taxes, less bureaucracy, a return to nuclear power. She entered the Bundestag in 2017, became party co-chair with Tino Chrupalla in June 2022, ran as chancellor candidate in February 2025, and since May 2025 has been co-leader of the opposition to Friedrich Merz. In July this year her party re-elected her with 81.3 per cent, unopposed, which in the AfD counts as a coronation.She also lives in Einsiedeln in Switzerland with her partner Sarah Bossard, a film producer born in Sri Lanka and adopted by a Swiss couple, with whom she is raising two sons, while the party she leads campaigns on traditional families and hard borders. Commentators have been calling this a contradiction since 2017, which is generous of them, because it may be closer to a division of labour. Björn Höcke and the party's radical wing supply the ideology and the court cases; Weidel supplies the CV, the fluency and the reassurance that nothing very frightening is going on. Someone has to be the acceptable face, and it helps enormously if the acceptable face genuinely believes she is one.The German state does not agree. The domestic intelligence agency classified the party as a confirmed right-wing extremist organisation in May 2025 after a report running past 1,100 pages, then suspended the label pending litigation; a court has since held that the agency may not use the "confirmed" tag, while the interior minister maintains that the party remains a legitimate object of observation. The AfD's own Saxony-Anhalt branch, the one that just won 43.9 per cent, is classified by that state's intelligence service as confirmed right-wing extremist. Weidel's answer, delivered each time with the patience of someone explaining a spreadsheet, is that the whole apparatus is politically motivated. Roughly six voters in Saxony-Anhalt out of ten disagreed with the classification enough not to care.What actually broke on Sunday was not the AfD's ceiling but the arithmetic of the Brandmauer, the firewall by which every other German party has refused coalition with the AfD. Chrupalla said the voters had struck it down, which is the sort of claim that sounds like spin until you count seats. To govern without the AfD, the CDU must assemble something delicate involving the Left party, which the CDU has also sworn never to touch. A firewall that requires two mutually exclusive vows is not a firewall; it is a scheduling conflict. Whether the AfD forms Germany's first far-right state government since 1945 or merely watches its opponents fail to form anything, the party gains, and both the Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern elections are two weeks away.For an Indian reader the temptation is to file this under European curiosities, which would be a mistake for two reasons. The first is practical: Germany is India's largest trading partner in the European Union and has spent three years courting Indian engineers, nurses and coders, and the politics of who is welcome there is now being written in Magdeburg rather than in Berlin ministries. The second is methodological. The lesson Weidel offers is not about immigration at all. It is that a movement the establishment considers unthinkable does not arrive wearing the uniform the establishment has been watching for. It arrives with a doctorate, a foreign posting, a mortgage in Switzerland and excellent manners, and it wins the argument about respectability long before it wins the vote.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: No royal duties: King Charles clarifies Harry and Meghan remain private citizens after UK return
articles.summary: UK News: King Charles clarifies that Prince Harry and Meghan remain private citizens and will not resume royal duties following their recent return to the UK. The couple's public engagements will not represent the Royal Family, and they will continue to use their personal titles only.
articles.body: Prince Harry and Meghan will not resume official royal duties despite returning to the UK, with a letter sent on behalf of King Charles confirming they remain private citizens.The message, issued by Lord Chamberlain, one of the senior officials at Buckingham Palace, has been sent to Harry’s team as well as government departments, military officials and Lord Lieutenants, sources told BBC.It makes clear that any public engagements undertaken by the Duke and Duchess of Sussex will be carried out in a personal capacity and will not represent the Royal Family.Harry and Meghan will also continue to be barred from using the “HRH” titles, or His and Her Royal Highness, despite their return to Britain with their children, Archie and Lilibet last month.The Palace position follows the arrangement agreed in 2020, when the couple stepped back from royal duties and moved to the US. The so-called Sandringham Agreement ruled out a role that would allow them to combine independent commercial activities with official work as members of the Royal Family.The letter says, “It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the Sovereign, and are no longer working members of the Royal Family.”It adds, “The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity.”The clarification comes as the couple are expected to make public appearances in Britain this autumn while supporting their charitable work.The letter also tells organisations planning events involving Harry and Meghan should contact Buckingham Palace if they have questions about arrangements, particularly when public money could be involved.Security remains a separate issue. The Palace said operational security matters should continue to be handled by the relevant police authorities.Harry has previously challenged the level of police protection available to him in Britain. articles.title: First road bridge between Russia, North Korea opens after years of planning
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Russia and North Korea have opened their first road bridge between the two countries, marking another step in their increasingly close relationship.Th.
articles.body: Russia and North Korea have opened their first road bridge between the two countries, marking another step in their increasingly close relationship.The 1-km, two-lane bridge crosses the Tumen River and was inaugurated on Monday in a ceremony attended virtually by Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song. The first trucks, carrying the flags of both countries, crossed the bridge as the two leaders addressed officials and workers by video link.New route to boost cross-border tradeThe bridge project had been discussed for several years before construction began in April last year. The decision to build it followed Russian President Vladimir Putin's visit to North Korea in 2024.Russia and North Korea already have direct air and rail connections. However, there had been no dedicated road crossing between the two countries.Since 1959, vehicles have been able to cross the border using planks laid on the existing rail bridge. That bridge, known as the Friendship Bridge, had remained the only border crossing between Russia and North Korea for decades.Mishustin said the new road connection would help expand cooperation between the two countries."I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a ​powerful impetus for ​the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation," said Mishustin, ⁠who said ties between Moscow and Pyongyang were "at an unprecedented high level" ​and called the opening of the bridge "a genuinely historic event."The Russian prime minister described the project as more than an infrastructure development, calling it "a new symbol of friendship".Up to 300 vehicles will be able to use the bridge each day, Mishustin said. It will connect to Russia's federal road network and provide access to the transport corridor linking Vladivostok in the Russian Far East with St Petersburg.Cargo trucks will start using the bridge immediately, according to the Russian government. The crossing is expected to become fully operational by the end of this year, when passenger traffic will also be allowed.Bridge named after Soviet soldierThe new bridge has been built close to the existing Friendship Bridge, which was opened in 1959 following the Korean War.It has been named after Yakov Novichenko, a Red Army soldier who is credited by North Korea with saving the life of its first leader, Kim Il Sung, in 1946. According to Pyongyang's account, Novichenko intercepted a grenade thrown towards Kim Il Sung and others.The opening comes as Moscow and Pyongyang have moved closer since Russia launched its war in Ukraine in 2022.North Korea has sent thousands of troops to Russia's Kursk region to help Russian forces fight a Ukrainian incursion that began in 2024.Mishustin referred to that cooperation during his speech, praising "the Korean heroes who, only recently, fought shoulder to shoulder with our soldiers and defended Russian soil".The new bridge therefore carries both practical and political significance for Moscow and Pyongyang, providing a new land route while underscoring the closer ties between the two governments.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1979, Paul McCartney bought a 151-acre Arizona ranch; the Beatles star turned it into a private family retreat
articles.summary: US News: In 1979, Paul McCartney and his wife Linda bought a secluded 151-acre ranch near Tucson, Arizona, creating a private escape far removed from the globa.
articles.body: In 1979, Paul McCartney and his wife Linda bought a secluded 151-acre ranch near Tucson, Arizona, creating a private escape far removed from the global attention surrounding one of music's most recognisable figures. Located near the foothills of the Rincon Mountains, the property gave the McCartney family something increasingly difficult to find, which was privacy. The ranch was not designed as a showpiece for celebrity life. Instead, its modest home, open desert surroundings and relative isolation offered a place where Paul, Linda and their children could spend time together away from cameras and crowds. Over the years, the Arizona property became closely connected with the family's life, from ordinary trips around Tucson to celebrations with friends and neighbours. It also remained deeply significant after Linda's death in 1998. Decades later, the ranch continues to represent a quieter and more personal side of McCartney's extraordinary life.Paul McCartney's 151-acre Arizona ranch was a private family retreatPaul and Linda McCartney bought the property in 1979, putting down roots near Tucson on a large stretch of land at the foothills of the Rincon Mountains. According to Architectural Digest, the main residence was a two-storey home with a tin roof and stucco exterior, and the setting offered the family privacy and peace. The property stood on Tucson's far north-eastern side, near Reddington Pass. ‘The Paul McCartney Project’ reports the ranch as a secluded escape. For a musician whose life had been shaped by the extraordinary fame of the Beatles, that separation from public attention mattered. The ranch was not simply another property in an extensive portfolio. It became a place where family life could take priority over celebrity.Linda's connection with Tucson gave the place a personal meaningThe decision to buy a ranch in southern Arizona also had a strong connection to Linda McCartney's past. According to Saddlebag Notes, Linda had studied at the University of Arizona and had developed an affection for Tucson's desert landscape and surrounding mountains. That personal attachment helped make the region more than a convenient location for a second home. The desert's rugged scenery, open space and quieter pace offered a sharp contrast to the cities and public environments that dominated much of Paul McCartney's professional life.A beautiful yet ordinary life unfolded beyond the ranch gatesDespite Paul McCartney's international fame, the family was not completely hidden away. According to Saddlebag Notes, Tucson residents generally gave the McCartneys their privacy while allowing them to move through the community with relative freedom. The family reportedly made ordinary trips to local shops and businesses. Paul was seen using an old pickup truck to collect ranch supplies. They also attended swap meets and visited local businesses.The McCartneys occasionally went to restaurants, grocery stores and petrol stations, greeting people they encountered along the way. Their ability to live without constant interference appeared to be part of what made Tucson so valuable to them. The family also invited friends and neighbours to holiday celebrations at the ranch. These small gatherings reflected the role the property played in their lives. The property was also a sanctuary where the McCartneys could ride horses, hike, swim and enjoy the surrounding desert. The family's four children also became part of this Arizona chapter of the McCartneys' story. That sense of normality was reinforced by the local community.The ranch became linked with profound loss of LindaThe Arizona retreat remained a central part of the McCartneys' lives until Linda McCartney's death in 1998. Architectural Digest reports that Paul still owns the ranch, which was also the site of her death. Linda had been diagnosed with breast cancer in December 1995 and received treatment in Arizona. She died on 17 April 1998 at the ranch, aged 56. The property came to hold memories of both the family's happiest years and one of its most painful moments. Neighbours saw Paul driving an old ranch Jeep across the isolated hills the day after Linda's death, appearing deeply grief-stricken.Even so, the family's connection with Tucson did not entirely disappear. Members of the McCartney family have continued to be seen in the area, while son James McCartney has spoken warmly about the desert and his mother's attachment to it, as reported by Saddlebag Notes. Nearly half a century after Paul and Linda bought the 151-acre property, the ranch remains a reminder that one of the world's most famous musicians also sought a place where his family could step away from the spotlight and simply live.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 9/11 suspect's al Qaida, Saudi links: New report claims FBI had key evidence, but didn't pursue
articles.summary: US News: Newly released videos show Omar al-Bayoumi, a Saudi national investigated by the FBI after the September 11, 2001 attacks, embracing future al Qaida l.
articles.body: Newly released videos show Omar al-Bayoumi, a Saudi national investigated by the FBI after the September 11, 2001 attacks, embracing future al Qaida leader Anwar al-Awlaki and taking part in paintball exercises with him, according to a BBC investigation.The footage, obtained by BBC Panorama and Radio 4, was among evidence gathered by investigators after the attacks but has never previously been made public. It forms part of a $1 trillion lawsuit filed by 9/11 families alleging Saudi Arabia was complicit in the attacks.One video, filmed near San Diego in 1997 or early 1998, shows Bayoumi and Awlaki participating in paintball exercises alongside an official from Saudi Arabia's ministry of Islamic affairs. Participants, some wearing military-style clothing, engage in mock urban combat and target practice, with some heard shouting "Allahu Akbar".According to the BBC, FBI investigators were later told that some participants used paintball sessions to train for jihad. Awlaki, who was killed in a US drone strike in 2011, already had links to al Qaida operatives at the time.Another previously unseen clip shows Bayoumi embracing Awlaki in January 1998. Bayoumi had denied meeting Awlaki during a 2021 deposition in the 9/11 families’ lawsuit. The video appears to contradict that claim.Bayoumi arrived in San Diego in 1994, claiming to be an English-language student. Investigators later found evidence suggesting he had largely abandoned his studies and was involved in organising religious activities.Bayoumi emerged as an early FBI suspect after his name was found on an apartment rental agreement signed by Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar, two of the hijackers who later helped crash a plane into the Pentagon.British police arrested Bayoumi in Birmingham on September 21, 2001, and seized thousands of documents, photographs and around 80 videotapes. Among the evidence was a handwritten diagram showing a plane alongside mathematical calculations relating to altitude and distance.The FBI obtained copies of the diagram within days of the attacks, but British detectives questioning Bayoumi were not briefed about it, despite the evidence being just metres away at the police station where he was held.A federal judge later said the document, on its face, “connects Bayoumi with knowledge of the 9/11 Attacks”, the BBC reported.The BBC also found that FBI agents in San Diego repeatedly sought evidence about Bayoumi but did not receive much of it, while attempts by FBI offices to interview some of his Saudi government contacts were blocked.Bayoumi was released on September 28, 2001, after US officials concluded there was insufficient evidence to seek his extradition.Bayoumi and the Saudi government have denied involvement in or prior knowledge of the attacks. Neither responded to the BBC’s requests for comment. The FBI declined to comment.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘Will reduce UP to Orwellian Dystopia’: Allahabad HC raps Noida DM over student’s NSA detention
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Allahabad High Court has ordered recovery of Rs 5 lakh from the salaries of the Gautam Buddha Nagar district magistrate and other offic.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Allahabad High Court has ordered recovery of Rs 5 lakh from the salaries of the Gautam Buddha Nagar district magistrate and other officials after quashing the National Security Act (NSA) detention of Delhi University student and activist Akriti Chaudhary.The division bench of Justices Atul Sreedharan and Achal Sachdev held that Chaudhary's detention violated her fundamental right to life and personal liberty under Article 21, finding that the material relied upon by authorities did not justify invoking the stringent preventive detention law.The court directed that Rs 5 lakh be paid to Chaudhary as compensation and recovered from the salary of Gautam Buddha Nagar DM Medha Roopam and other officers found responsible, including the SHO who prepared the initial report backing her detention. It also directed that the court's displeasure with the officials be entered in their service records.In a strongly worded September 2 order, the court criticised the manner in which the detention order was passed and warned that continued "despotic" conduct by "errant" bureaucrats could reduce Uttar Pradesh to an "Orwellian Dystopia", reported PTI.Chaudhary, a 24-year-old history graduate, was arrested in connection with cases arising from a workers' protest in Noida in April 2026. The UP Police invoked the NSA against her and activist-journalist Satya Verma on May 13. They were among activists arrested in cases related to the protest seeking higher wages.The court said the police dossier against Chaudhary contained allegations but lacked credible supporting material. It said the DM was required to independently examine the record before deciding whether preventive detention was warranted."The conduct of the Gautam Buddha Nagar DM who passed the impugned order is worthy of derision," the court said.The bench noted that Chaudhary had no previous criminal record and that there was no material showing she had incited violence. It said the circumstances suggested that the detention was intended to make an example of her and discourage others from exercising their right to freedom of speech and expression in support of labourers.The court also questioned the state's version of when Chaudhary was arrested. It recorded that she was taken into custody around 5.30 pm on April 11 at Botanical Garden Metro Station, although the state claimed her arrest took place on April 12.A notice issued under Section 130 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) was cited by the state. However, the notice carried General Diary Entry No. 37, which was generated only at 10.20 am on April 12."Mentioning the GD number in the notice under section 130 of the BNSS reveals that the petitioner was already arrested and the procedure of giving a notice under section 130 of the BNSS was ex post facto the arrest and nothing more than a sham," Justice Sreedharan said."I agree with the view of brother Justice Achal Sachdev that the notice u/s. 130 of the BNSS was prepared after the arrest of the Petitioner and that is the reason why the time of issuance is not mentioned in the notice and its omission is deliberate," he added.The court said preventive detention under the NSA is an exception and cannot be used in place of ordinary criminal law. It described the grounds of Chaudhary's detention as "repetitive, speculative and are only opinion-based", noting the absence of material supporting those conclusions.It also cautioned authorities against treating peaceful public protests as a threat merely because they could potentially lead to a breach of peace."Preventing people from gathering in public spaces or agitating for their rights on the grounds of assumed breach of peace would be throwing the baby out of the bath water," the court said.The bench said the constitutional protection of freedom of speech and expression extends to peaceful gatherings and collective action, and cannot be curtailed merely on the basis of the state's subjective assessment.The court also reminded bureaucrats and police officers that their duty is to the Constitution rather than the political executive, saying that people are the masters in a democracy.It warned that officials who disregard their constitutional oath could come to be seen as an "oppressive vestige of the British Empire", creating an environment of civil unrest.The court said the judiciary could pass "harsh orders" to compensate citizens where official excesses or illegalities infringe upon civil liberties without adequate cause or due process.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: The Solheim Cup 2026: All you need to know as Europe host US
articles.summary: All you need to know as Europe gets ready to host the United States in the 20th edition of the Solheim Cup at Bernardus Golf in the Netherlands.
articles.body:
The 20th edition of the Solheim Cup takes place between 11-13 September as Europe host the United States at Bernardus Golf in the Netherlands.

Europe are looking to regain the trophy after losing 15½-12½ in Virginia two years ago in the biggest team competition in women's golf.

BBC Sport will have live radio commentary on 5 Live Sports Extra 3 across all three days - which is now also available via most smart speakers - and daily highlights on television.

There will also be live text commentary, video highlights, reaction and analysis on the BBC Sport website and mobile app.

The Solheim Cup is a biennial match that is played over three days, between two teams of 12 women from Europe and the United States.

It is named in honour of the Norwegian-American golf club manufacturer Karsten Solheim and his wife Louise, who have sponsored the event since its inaugural contest in 1990, and have also played a huge part in supporting the women's game over the past 50 years.

The US have won the trophy 11 times, Europe have won seven and there has been one tie - the dramatic 14-14 draw at Finca Cortesin in Spain in 2023.

Who will captain Europe & the United States?

Both teams are under new leadership, with Anna Nordqvist captaining Europe and Angela Stanford, who has served as an assistant captain three times, taking the helm for the United States.

Three-time major champion Nordqvist, who announced her retirement as a player in August, will be assisted by fellow Swede Caroline Hedwall and Dutch golfer Anne van Dam.

Mel Reid also be part of Nordqvist's staff after previously taking on a similar role for Catriona Matthew in 2019 at Gleneagles and Suzann Pettersen at the Robert Trent Jones Golf Club, two years ago.

Kristy McPherson, Paula Creamer and Brittany Lang, who all played in the 2009 edition with Stanford, make up the backroom team for the United States.

With English pair Lottie Woad and Charley Hull in their ranks Europe go into the contest boasting more players inside the top 10 in the world than their opponents.

Woad and Hull were among the eight automatic qualifiers for Europe's team.

They are joined by France's Celine Boutier, Carlota Ciganda of Spain, Germany's Esther Henseleit and Swedish duo Maja Stark and Linn Grant and Denmark's Nanna Koerstz Madsen.

Ireland's Leona Maguire, Spain's Julia Lopez Ramirez, France's Nastasia Nadaud and England's Mimi Rhodes compete the line-up for Europe.

In Nelly Korda, the United States can field the current world number one, who has won two major championships this season.

Korda, who triumphed at the Chevron Championship in April and the US Women's Open in June, was an automatic qualifier for the 12-strong team alongside Angel Yin, Jennifer Kupcho, Yealimi Noh, Auston Kim, Lauren Coughlin and Allisen Corpuz.

Andrea Lee and Alison Lee will also feature for the US by virtue of their places in the world rankings, while Stanford named Megan Khang, Rose Zhang and Lindy Duncan as her captain's picks.

What's the Solheim Cup format and scoring?

There will be 28 matchplay matches over three days in foursomes, fourballs and singles. Each match is worth one point with half a point awarded to both teams if they are tied.

The team who gets to 14½ points first wins the Solheim Cup outright. As current holders, the US will retain the trophy if the contest was to end in a 14-14 draw.

Foursomes - there are four matches, played in pairs, on Friday and Saturday. Each pair uses one ball hitting alternate shots with the lowest score on each hole winning.

Fourballs - there are four matches, played in pairs, on Friday and Saturday. All four players use their own ball The lowest scoring ball on each hole from each side is taken.

On Sunday all 24 players from both teams compete in 12 singles matches.

Temperatures will peak at around 21C over the three days of competition on the heathland course that only opened in 2018.

However, there is also a strong likelihood of showers and breezy conditions which will provide an added layer of difficulty on a course that demands precision.

Bernardus Golf hosted the DP World Tour's KLM Open between 2021-2023.

How to follow the Solheim Cup on the BBC

19:30-20:00 BST: Solheim Cup preview programme on BBC Radio 5 Live

06:30-17:00: Live text commentary on BBC Sport website and app, with updates on BBC Radio 5 Live

13:00: Live radio commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra 3 and BBC Sport website and app

10:00-close of play: Live text commentary on BBC Sport website and app

11:00-close of play: Live radio commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra 3 and BBC Sport website and app

You can also follow live and uninterrupted on most smart speakers.

On Friday, just tell your device to 'ask BBC Sounds to play Solheim Cup - day one'. For Saturday's coverage, you'll need to ask for 'day two', and on Sunday ask for 'day three'.
